#3453. 10 Shows Like 'Cyberpunk: Edgerunners' You Should Watch Next

Ross Johnson writes about television, film, and literature for Lifehacker. He has a degree in political science from the University of Rochester and has previously been a legal writer and editor for Thomson Reuters, for which he later traveled around India and the Middle East as an educator specializing in American English style and grammar for adults.

Ross has been an actor on stage, in commercials, and in independent films since childhood, and has written hundreds of articles and essays on genre literature and cinema for Barnes & Noble, Gizmodo, Kotaku, and Yahoo! Entertainment.Ross produces the Swan Songs film podcast and hosts The Sound of Tomorrow, a pop culture and current affairs radio show based in Rochester, New York, where he lives with his husband and dogs and supports the local arts and cinema scene. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Following the dramatic conclusion of Cyberpunk: Edgerunners way back in 2022, the show has returned for a new season set in the megalopolis of Night City with a standalone story and a new cast of characters (by necessity).

Though the aesthetic and themes of cyberpunk have their roots in American science fiction of the 1970s and '80s, anime and manga of the '90s and beyond embraced the form and took it to entirely new places—so much so that a Japanese/Polish co-production of an adaptation of a video game from a Polish designer has taken its cues from a couple of decades' worth of great anime and cerebral sci-fi. Which is to say, if you're looking for more heady sci-fi series, these 10 are a good place to start.

An iconic, effortlessly cool genre classic, Cowboy Bebop is one of the undisputed GOATs of anime, blending western, noir, and crime genres and setting the resultant mash to a killer soundtrack of old-school jazz (which serves much the same purpose as Cyberpunk's propulsive electronic grooves). The title's "cowboys" are bounty hunters in a near-future in which humans have been forced to colonize the solar system after Earth became uninhabitable. Different settings, but both shows offer up ragtag crews with highly dubious fates. Former hitman Spike Spiegel leads his crew on one nearly disastrous mission after another, their standalone adventures all building to a thoroughly memorable climax. Stream Cowboy Bebop on Crunchyroll or buy it from Prime Video.

This one's set in 22nd-century Japan, with a slick Blade Runner-esque aesthetic and a setup reminiscent of Minority Report. Here, technology exists to measure intentions, so crimes can be stopped before they’ve occurred, at which point the “criminals” are placed into psychological treatment (à la A Clockwork Orange)—or subject to summary execution because their threat potential is too high. That ability to predict behavior bleeds over into every aspect of life: careers and even relationships are determined in large part by the same systems that sniff out criminal intent. Obviously, this is all perfectly fine, and there’s no potential for abuse or miscalculation whatsoever...though there are a couple of warning signs. The first involves a new Enforcer who becomes a potential murderer himself when he miscalculates the extent of a criminal’s potential to do wrong, and, even more significantly, the existence of a criminal mastermind who is somehow invisible to the tech, even as his criminal actions grow more and more elaborate. Stream Psycho-Pass on Prime Video and Crunchyroll.

Created by Tim Miller and with director David Fincher as an executive producer, this animated anthology series is a grab bag of wildly diverse offerings: Each episode is produced by a different international studio, with the only link between them being one of the three words in the show's title. One episode deals with robotic gladiator fights in dystopian London, another finds us under the threat of sentient yogurt, yet another finds an ambitious cat learning to make use of a family's robot helper. Its format dictates that no two episodes are going to have the same premise, but it shares with Cyberpunk an edgy sensibility and stories set in an apocalyptic future, albeit with a dark sense of humor—its four seasons offer up a mix of tech, sex, violence, and gorgeous animation. Stream Love, Death & Robots on Netflix.

One of several completely standalone spinoffs of the wildly influential 1995 film (itself based on the beloved manga series), Stand Alone Complex requires no prior knowledge. The style is largely the draw, as the series luxuriates in its fictional Nihama City setting, a world unto itself in a future Japan in which cybernetic people hack directly into the internet. Our sympathies are more with the authorities—in this case, Public Security Section 9, a cybercrime and antiterrorism police unit—than the cyber criminals, but the show approaches some of the same themes as Edgerunners with legit punk style. Stream Ghost in the Shell: Stand Alone Complex on Tubi and The Criterion Channel.

In this adaptation of the Richard K. Morgan cyberpunk classic of the same name, Joel Kinnaman and Anthony Mackie (yes, both of them) star as Takeshi "Tak" Kovacs. In this future megacity setting, human consciousness can be transferred between bodies. The tech is widely available, but only the wealthy can afford the backups and protections that make it a form of virtual immortality. Kovacs is a former soldier turned mercenary, revived from a backup after 200 years by Laurens Bancroft (James Purefoy), one of the wealthiest men alive. His motives for bringing the man back are shrouded in mystery, but he's giving Tak a chance to solve a very cold case: his own murder. Stream Altered Carbon on Netflix.

Another popular (and Emmy-winning) game adaptation, Arcane is based on League of Legends, a top-down actioner involving online opponents shooting lasers across a map. It doesn't sound like fodder for a show this impressive, but here we are. The League of Legends lore forms the backdrop for the show, but the pull is in the narrative involving two sisters caught up in the growing conflict between a utopian city and its oppressed underclass, without whom it couldn’t exist. The painted animation style is truly something special—not a stylistic match for Cyberpunk, but the two shows both go far above and beyond to create striking visual worlds. Stream Arcane on Netflix.

Vash the Stampede is a hunted outcast with a dark history that slowly comes to light over the course of the series. He’s got a reputation as a human wrecking ball, bringing destruction wherever he goes, and seemingly just for fun—but in reality he’s far more respectful of life than his pursuers. Still, cities evacuate at the mere possibility of his arrival, and a huge bounty sits on his head (no matter that the bounty hunters do far more damage than Vash). He and his friends—actually a couple of insurance agents—find themselves in a series of misadventures on the planet Gunsmoke, building to a final showdown that caps the series with finality. Visually, it’s probably one of the defining ‘90s shōnen-style action series, with elegantly choreographed gunfights that never get old. Tonally similar, Trigun also shares with Cyberpunk 2 the work of legendary composer Tsuneo Imahori, his music being crucial to both shows. Stream Trigun on Crunchyroll or buy it from Prime Video.

Another from animation studio Trigger, Darling in the Franxx leans heavily into the mecha sub-genre, set in a post-apocalypse where children are bred and indoctrinated into piloting the title's massive Franxx to defend the remnants of humanity. Adults are pretty much immortal, so the kids simply don't have any other utility. Two of these teens begin to develop romantic feelings for each other, potentially complicating their usefulness to society and leading to an explosive, bittersweet finale. Stream Darling in the Franxx on Crunchyroll or buy it from Prime Video.

What starts out as a relatively straightforward action show about space bounty hunters (the title's “Killjoys”) develops surprising depth over the course of its five seasons. As officially sanctioned Killjoys, the trio at the show’s heart (Hannah John-Kamen, Aaron Ashmore, and Luke Macfarlane) are bound to remain politically neutral at any cost. Initially, that’s a way to get them right into the heat of a fight, but as they develop ties of friendship and family in an exploited community, they come to understand the high cost of unchecked wealth and greed, and the ways in which neutrality always benefits the oppressors. The show’s creators make exceptionally good use of a limited budget and offer up some impressive queer rep along the way, a rarity in pop sci-fi. Stream Killjoys on Tubi or buy it from Prime Video and Apple TV.

Another great cyberpunk metropolis: here it's Kansai, an increasingly lawless city run by elite criminals known as Akudama. An ordinary girl, quite inadvertently, becomes caught up in a major planned heist and is forced to fake credentials as a master swindler in order to stay alive. Like Cyberpunk, the show tackles anti-authoritarian themes among a diverse crew of outsiders. Stream Akudama Drive on Cunrchyroll or buy it from Prime Video.

Something is seriously wrong with Microsoft Outlook and other popular Microsoft services like Teams, Microsoft 365, Copilot and others. More than 100,000 users are flocking to the popular outage-reporting website Downdetector to report issues.

Reports began to emerge yesterday at around 12:00 pm ET and although reports have dropped, there are still widespread problems across Microsoft's products.

For its part, Microsoft has posted on X to its Microsoft 365 Status account about the issue and what it's doing to get things back in order. I eventually got the Microsoft 365 status page to load, and it's been keeping us updated on the latest issues.

There's been another small drop in the number of reports on Downdetector, but it's still a sizable number.

We’re seeing continued recovery progress across affected regions, with broader improvements in North America, sustained improvements across much of Europe, and encouraging recovery signals in Asia Pacific. Microsoft posted that it's seeing good recovery progress for users, though some people may still have issues.

"We’re seeing continued recovery progress across affected regions, with broader improvements in North America, sustained improvements across much of Europe, and encouraging recovery signals in Asia Pacific. Some users may still experience intermittent access issues or delayed email delivery as mitigation continues across remaining affected infrastructure. Our focus remains on stabilizing recovered infrastructure, completing mitigation in remaining impacted areas, and reducing delayed email queues and backlogs while we validate service consistency across connection methods," the company said on its Microsoft 365 X account.

If you're still dealing with Outlook issues, drop me an email and let know what's happening. My email is dave.leclair@futurenet.com and I'd like to hear to about what kinds of issues are still happening out there.

The only thing to report at the moment is that there's nothing new to report. Microsoft hasn't posted any updates in about an hour, and the Downdetector reports are still hovering around 10,000.

While it's gone down a little, the number of reports is still hanging around 10,000, which means a sizable amount of Outlook users are still dealing with issues.

We’re seeing encouraging recovery progress, with service availability and email delivery performance improving across a growing portion of affected Microsoft 365 infrastructure. We’re focused on recovery for the remaining affected environments while prioritizing email queue and backlog reduction. Microsoft says it's seeing some good progress towards putting this outage to bed, but we're not quite out of the woods yet. Here's the latest update from Microsoft 365's X account:

"We’re seeing encouraging recovery progress, with service availability and email delivery performance improving across a growing portion of affected Microsoft 365 infrastructure. Some users may still experience intermittent issues as recovery actions continue. We’re focused on recovery for the remaining affected environments while prioritizing email queue and backlog reduction. The extended 48-hour email timeout window remains in place to help protect delayed messages as delivery catches up."

On the U.S. version of Downdetector, reports are hanging steadily at around 13,000. They got as low as 4,000 during the overnight stretch, but that's likely due to a large portion of North American readers being asleep.

"We’re seeing encouraging recovery progress in Europe, with service availability and email delivery performance improving across a growing portion of affected Microsoft 365 infrastructure. Japan remains comparatively more stable, while North America is also improving; however, some users may still experience intermittent issues as recovery actions continue.

We're focused on addressing the remaining areas of disruption and improving service consistency across affected regions. Reducing email queues and backlogs remains a priority, and the extended 48-hour email timeout window remains in place to help protect delayed messages as delivery catches up.

At this time, we have no evidence of malicious activity associated with this incident. We will continue to treat this with urgency until full mitigation, and we will share a full Post-Incident Report with root cause and defense-in-depth actions after mitigation is complete," reads Microsoft's most recent status update.

The reports over on DownDetector are shrinking, and they've fallen a long way from yesterday's peak. But I'm still seeing them at over 4,000 at time of writing. I don't think we're out of the woods yet...

Microsoft's fixes aren't exactly going as expected, which means a lot of people who need these products for either their home or work are going to have a very disrupted Friday. Are you still experiencing problems with any Microsoft systems? Let me know where you're based and how you're coping.

If you have an alternative to Outlook, you can email me at jeff.parsons@futurenet.com or add a comment below this article.

Microsoft's products are used by a lot of companies, and today's outage will not be helping their Friday productivity much.

“Microsoft has confirmed there is no indication that this outage was caused by a cyber attack, but the disruption is a stark reminder of just how reliant we've become on digital infrastructure and how quickly everyday operations can grind to a halt when critical systems go offline," Marijus Briedis, Chief Technology Officer at NordVPN, told Tom's Guide

“The scale of this outage highlights just how interconnected our digital world has become. When a major technology platform experiences disruption, the knock-on effects can spread rapidly across businesses, industries and essential services, affecting millions of people who rely on these systems every day.

"This should be a wake-up call for every organisation. Businesses need to ensure they can continue operating when critical technology becomes unavailable, without relying entirely on a single system or provider.”

Microsoft says the cause of these problems isn't down to a cyber attack.

"At this time, we are not aware of any malicious activity causing this incident," the company wrote in its latest status update.

"We will continue to treat this with urgency until full mitigation, and we will share a full Post-Incident Report with root cause and defense-in-depth actions after recovery is complete."

Hi everyone, Jeff Parsons here from Tom's Guide's U.K. office, stepping in to this live blog to keep you updated.

We're into the second day of this Microsoft outage, and the knock-on effects are being felt over this side of the pond.

Many schools across the country use Microsoft's services and are now relying on phone lines. Banks and hospitals are also affected. Even the government is wrapped up in the Microsoft blanket. A U.K. parliamentary spokesperson told the BBC: “We are aware of the global issue affecting Microsoft email services, which is impacting users of the parliamentary network. We are working with Microsoft to resolve the matter as quickly as possible.

"Alternative communication arrangements are in place, allowing today’s business to continue.”

Microsoft's latest update says the company is extending the email timeout window on Outlook to 48 hours as it continues to grapple with the problems.

This just means the email client will wait a bit longer to receive emails so that anything sent from an unaffected service, like Gmail, will still arrive after the problem is fixed.

It's been over 15 hours since reports first emerged, and Microsoft has posted an update to its status page explaining that, "service capacity has not yet returned to normal levels."

"Recovery efforts are ongoing across impacted infrastructure," the company wrote. "We are seeing early signs of stabilization, but service capacity has not yet returned to normal levels and health remains variable as traffic is carefully reintroduced."

This has been a very long outage, and it's still going, with more than 25,000 reports on Downdetector. While we're far away from where it was when it peaked, we're clearly still not out of the situation fully.

We'll keep you updated as the outage develops, whether it's Microsoft fixing everything fully or the issues continuing.

According to a post on X from Microsoft, the company is warning users that the servers that led to today's outage "can become unresponsive again once they receive traffic." For this reason, Microsoft is "limiting which types of traffic can reach affected infrastructure in some locations" which explains why we're still seeing around 30,000 reports of issues with Outlook on Downdetector.~~~

Today's Outlook outage does appear to be winding down with the issue being at least partially resolved for some. However, there are still almost 30,000 reports on Downdetector at the time of writing at 7:12pm ET. We're going to stay on top of this to let you know once Outlook is fully back up and running.

As of right now at 5:38pm ET, the number of users reporting issues with Outlook on Downdetector is declining. However, there are still over 30,000 reports of problems with the service.

Since Microsoft Outlook outages tend to happen several times a year or more, once it's fully restored, you might want to consider exporting your contacts to a CSV file. That way, when the next outage happens, you can switch to a different email provider in the meantime.Now this won't help if you need to login to Outlook just to user your work account. In Outlook itself, you can export your contacts by going to Open & Export and then Import/Export. Select Export to a file, then Comma Separated Values (CSV) and click next. After selecting your contacts and hitting Finish, all of your Outlook contacts will be available as a separate file you can import into Gmail, Yahoo Mail, etc.

I don't think we're out of the woods just yet, but it's a good sign that reports are declining on Downdetector. As of 5:41 pm ET the number was just over 37,000. Some users are reporting that Outlook is back up.

Having Microsoft Outlook go down during the middle of a workday is never fun for anyone. However, today's outage is far from the worst one the service has experienced yet.Back in July of last year, Outlook was down for 19 to 21 hours worldwide and then in August of this year, it took 67 hours for Microsoft to fully fix the issue behind that outage. Hopefully Outlook returns to normal operations before the start of the workday tomorrow.

As those affected by today's Microsoft Outlook outage look for alternatives, users are now reporting problems at Gmail, Zoom and even Yahoo Mail on Downdetector. Meanwhile, the actual Outlook outage appears to be winding down at 4:45pm ET today as Microsoft has restarted the affected servers. At the time of writing though, there are still 50,000+ reports of users having problems with Outlook. So we're not in the clear yet.....

Here is the latest update from Microsoft's Office 365 status page:"We've validated an alternative health check method on a subset of affected infrastructure, which allowed the servers in that subset to successfully return to service, and we're now applying this change more broadly. We're also preparing an automated recovery process to continually detect and restart unresponsive servers, to help keep them in service while this change progresses. Additionally, our review of recent changes has identified a small number of configuration updates that we're investigating as potential contributors to the issue."

The problem isn't just related to Outlook, as Teams, Copilot, Defender XDR and more Microsoft services are affected. Some users have also reported being unable to access their OneDrive storage or Office online. Microsoft is restarting its servers with a fix in place, the company says.

As of 3:50 pm ET today, Downdetector shows 59595 reports. Although this is down from the peak of over 130K reports four hours ago, it is still a significant number.

Wendy's X account sure is something to behold. The fast-food brand is dropping some hilarious takes about the outage in its replies to users, including a timely reference to it being down because "that guy cheated on his wife."

Microsoft posted another update on its status page and it seems like things are moving forward but with some issues.

"While validating the targeted change, we found that many of the affected servers have become unresponsive, which is preventing us from confirming whether the change is effective. We're restarting these servers so they can come back online with the change in place, and we're applying the same approach to additional affected portions of our infrastructure to validate the results more broadly," reads the status page.

Lately, we haven't seen any significant drops in Downdetector reports. Currently, reports are at 61,000, and they've been gradually dropping. Usually, when something is fixed during an outage, we see a sharp drop in the number of reports; a gradual decline likely indicates that people just aren't reporting as much as when the outage first started.

"While we haven't identified any recent changes that correlate with the start of impact, our investigation indicates the failed health checks may originate from a specific component on the affected servers that's responsible for processing them. We're deploying a targeted change to bypass this component on a subset of servers to validate whether this restores availability, and we've taken steps to prevent additional servers from being removed from service while we work to return the affected servers to service. We're also investigating why affected servers are experiencing elevated processor usage while handling requests."

As usual, Reddit users have some funny takes on the outage. Not many of them are particularly helpful, but if you're looking for some entertainment while you can't get things done, it might be worth checking out this thread and having a laugh.

Of course, if you have your own witty comments, you're welcome to scroll down this page and leave a comment here; we read them all!

We've not identified any recent change correlated with the start of impact; however, our investigation indicates the failed health checks may originate from a specific component that's responsible for processing server health. We've taken steps to prevent additional servers from being impacted while we work to return the affected servers to service. More info under EX1550543 and MO1550821 in the Microsoft 365 admin center, as well as https://t.co/pYdahqxDv3 if the admin center is not available to you.November 12, 2026

Microsoft jumped on its 365 Status X account with another update, this time it said, "We've not identified any recent change correlated with the start of impact; however, our investigation indicates the failed health checks may originate from a specific component that's responsible for processing server health. We've taken steps to prevent additional servers from being impacted while we work to return the affected servers to service."

It sounds like it's doing what it can to mitigate the damage caused by the servers being down, but it doesn't have a solution to bring the affected one back online yet.

Finding useful messages in the Downdetector comments section is challenging, to say the least. When these outages happen, users tend to use the comments as a message board of sorts where they let out all kinds of random thoughts. This one is no exception.

However, some users are reporting actual statuses and information if you're willing to dig through all the memes and jokes. For example, the users in the screenshot above are currently dealing with issues in California, which isn't surprising since it seems to be hitting everywhere.

So far, 99% of the people who've voted in the poll above are experiencing issues with Outlook. Given that it has thousands of votes in that direction, I think it's pretty clear we aren't done with this outage yet.

"We're testing a configuration change to address a problem that's causing servers to fail automated health checks and become unavailable. In parallel, we've initiated a restart of all affected servers and are monitoring health as they return to service," the company posted on X and to its status page.

Reports have hit the 77,000 range recently, which is a sizable drop from the peak. It's still one of the bigger outage numbers we've seen in recent months, so we're by no means out of the woods yet, but between slightly lower reports and Microsoft having a strong idea of what went wrong, we could be in good shape.

We determined the elevated load isn't driven by an increase in traffic, but by a number of servers being unexpectedly unavailable; straining the remaining infrastructure. We're working to safely return them to service. More info under EX1550543 and MO1550821 in the Microsoft 365 admin center, as well as https://t.co/pYdahqxDv3 if the admin center is not available to you.November 12, 2026

"We determined the elevated load isn't driven by an increase in traffic, but by a number of servers being unexpectedly unavailable; straining the remaining infrastructure. We're working to safely return them to service," the company posted on X.

If Microsoft is able to get these servers up and running soon, we could be seeing this outage come to an end. Of course, it could take some time or end up being something else causing problems.

"We're aggressively pursuing all pathways to reduce impact. As a precaution, we've paused all deployments and configuration changes while we review recent changes for any correlation to this event. We've determined that the elevated load isn't driven by an overall increase in traffic, but by a large number of servers being unexpectedly unavailable, which is shifting load onto the remaining infrastructure. We're investigating what's causing these servers to become unavailable while we work to safely return them to service," reads the latest update on Microsoft's status page.

Downdetector reports are staying fairly steady with around 88,000 reports. That's about 10,000 down from the peak, but still a fairly high number.

Digging a little deeper into Microsoft's status page, we can see that the company says it has "completed redistributing connection traffic across our worldwide infrastructure, and we're moving additional traffic off the affected infrastructure to further reduce load." That sounds like a big step in the right direction for getting things back in working order.

"We're also restarting affected servers to return them to service. In parallel, we're investigating whether the elevated traffic reflects a genuine increase in requests or a shift in how traffic is being routed across our infrastructure," the status update continues.

We'll see if things start to come back to normal for Outlook and other Microsoft users (officially, Microsoft lists Exchange Online, Microsoft Teams,SharePoint Online, Microsoft Copilot 365 and Microsoft Defender XDR as affected services).

I decided to just leave the status page loading in the background without refreshing or anything. After about 5 minutes, I went back to the tab and saw that it finally loaded (probably took extra time due to whatever techniques Microsoft is using to re-route traffic).

Is this a sign that the outage is almost over? Maybe, but according to the now-loading status page, things are still very much not over.

While user reports are dropping, I personally still can't access the status page for Microsoft, so I'm forced to turn to X for the latest news (which isn't always as quick as going straight to the source). I've tried reloading the status page many times, and it's had the same result.

Of course, we'll continue to monitor both the status page and X for the latest information. When the status page does start working again, that's probably a good sign.

Downdetector reports have dropped below 100,000 for Outlook, which likely means that some of Microsoft's traffic-redistribution methods are working for at least some percentage of users.

We've begun redistributing connection traffic across our broader worldwide infrastructure to help balance the load. More info under EX1550543 and MO1550821 in the Microsoft 365 admin center, as well as https://t.co/uFnnN6Svuf if the admin center is not available to you.November 12, 2026

Microsoft appears to have found the cause, as it posted on X saying that "We've determined a portion of infrastructure is experiencing elevated load across multiple regions, which is likely contributing to the connectivity errors." It quickly followed up with another post saying, "We've begun redistributing connection traffic across our broader worldwide infrastructure to help balance the load."

It sounds like the company might have a solution to the problem, though I have to assume that redistributing that much traffic will take some time, so it might be a while before everything is working flawlessly.

While Outlook is getting the most attention in terms of raw reports, it's actually the whole of Microsoft 365 that's having problems, so other services are also experiencing outages that are impacting users, just not at the same scale as Outlook.

While we're working to mitigate impact, we've confirmed the issue may affect Microsoft 365 service connectivity for users in any region, more information will be provided in the Microsoft 365 admin center under EX1550543.November 12, 2026

Microsoft is aware of the issue and working on it. The company took to X to update users that it's "working to mitigate impact" and has "confirmed the issue may affect Microsoft 365 service connectivity for users in any region."

It didn't provide an updated time for when everything would be back to normal, but hopefully it can get things sorted quickly so emails and calendar alerts can start going again.

As of this post, Microsoft Outlook is sitting at more about 119,000 reports on Downdetector, which is a bit down from the peak of 130,000 but still a staggeringly large number of people having an issue with the productivity service.

#3450. 3 Elite Netflix Series to Binge This Weekend (Nov 14-15)

Another week of streaming has come to an end, and it's the return of a fantasy favorite that is dominating the headlines. After a shaky second season, The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power returned this week, trying to find form once again. Although Collider's Therese Lacson called Season 3 "a story that's finally worthy of J.R.R. Tolkien's sprawling universe," this latest installment has so far earned the lowest average critics' score on Rotten Tomatoes in the series. So if you don't plan on watching The Rings of Power, what should you watch instead? To help you decide, here's a look at three shows you should binge-watch on Netflix this weekend.

For more recommendations, check out our list of the best shows and movies on Netflix.

Disclaimer: These titles are available on US Netflix.

Of all the new titles on streaming this weekend, this should be the first on your radar. The Body, which is already earning comparisons to Stephen King's Carrie, stars Kristina Bogic and Sara Boustany as Anya and Elise, two of a group of misbehaving Catholic school girls whose lives change when they start to inexplicably experience prophetic visions, sending their town into chaos.

"The Body is like nothing else on streaming right now," wrote Gabrielle Moss in Collider's review, one of several glowing responses to this new series that have helped it reach a perfect 100% on Rotten Tomatoes. Sofia Wylie, Geena Meszaros, Shirley Chen, and The Traitors' winner Gabby Windey also star in this series, which is guaranteed to find its way to the top of the Netflix streaming charts. Don't miss out on the bandwagon this weekend.

Four franchises, four completely different ways of getting underneath your skin. This is the one built out of your particular fear, why it works so well on you, and what it would leave behind.

Your nightmare does not wait outside the door. It waits for you to close your eyes, which you are going to have to do eventually, because nobody has ever won that particular argument.

Your nightmare is not really the doll. It is the face of the person you tell, and the way they decide, very kindly, that you have imagined all of it.

Your nightmare has your number, knows your name, and has almost certainly been inside your house before. The worst part is that you already know them.

Your nightmare is not really about you. It is about the people asleep down the hall, and the feeling that whatever is here is not interested in leaving.

After coming to an end on CBS with its eighth season earlier this year, sitcom favorite The Neighborhood made the move to Netflix earlier this month. Created by Jim Reynolds, this cozy series stars Max Greenfield and Cedric the Entertainer as next-door neighbors who, despite their opposing personalities, become unlikely friends after the former moves to a predominantly Black neighborhood in Los Angeles.

A welcoming, heartwarming series packed with humor and not to be taken too seriously, The Neighborhood is a perfect option to keep your weekend light. Over eight seasons, the show premiered 155 episodes and even earned a Primetime Emmy nomination earlier this year for Outstanding Picture Editing for a Multi-Camera Comedy Series. With so many episodes available, there's no better time to finish a binge-watch than now.

One of the most exciting Netflix releases last month might've fallen under your radar, so why not make up for lost time this weekend and binge-watch Below? Written and created by The Umbrella Academy's Jesse McKeown, the series follows Josh Hartnett as fisherman Calvin, who must fight to defend his humble community from the threat of a mysterious sea creature.

Charlie Heaton (Stranger Things), Mackenzie Davis (The Martian), Ruby Stokes (Rocks), and more star alongside Verity's Hartnett in a series bursting with tension. "By the time you've concluded your own visit to Below, you might not be tempted to return, but you won't regret spending a weekend there," wrote Collider's Carly Lane, who awarded it a 7/10 in her review, so why not do just that and indulge in all six episodes now?

#3449. Five Smartwatch Heart Rate Zone Hacks Every Runner Should Know

If you've spent any time in or around running culture over the last few years, you've undoubtedly encountered someone preaching the gospel of Zone 2 cardio. Legend has it that easy, conversational effort cardio—also known as cardio that takes your heart rate into "Zone 2"—is the secret to unlocking everything from a bigger aerobic engine to faster race times and even a longer life.

To train by heart rate, you aim to keep your heart rate in the "zone" that gives you the desired workout. The catch is that Zone 2 is easy to get wrong, especially since no one can agree on what it actually means.  Your smartwatch can show you your heart rate, but many recreational runners will still drift into a “gray zone” that's too fast to be truly easy, and too slow to give them a real workout. If you're struggling to hit Zone 2 consistently, there are a few smartwatch hacks that can help.

Pace can be a distraction during easy runs, especially considering all the different variables that affect your effort, like hills, humidity, and general fatigue. A 9:30 mile might be Zone 2 on a flat, cool day and Zone 4 on a hot, hilly one.

Dig into your watch's activity settings (on Garmin, it's Activity > Data Screens; on Apple Watch, the Workout app's metrics layout; on Coros, Polar, and Suunto, similar menus) and put live heart rate zone front and center, ideally as a zone number or colored gauge rather than just a raw bpm figure (though this assumes these zones are accurate—more on that below).

Create an alert when your heart rate goes above or below a target range, delivered as a vibration pattern, a beep, or both. Set the alert for the upper boundary of Zone 2, and you've essentially hired a mini coach who taps you on the wrist whenever you get overzealous. Whenever you hear or feel that buzz, you’ll know you need to ease into a slower jog until your heart rate settles.

Instead of free-running and checking your numbers afterward, build structured workouts that carry the targets for you. In Garmin Connect, TrainingPeaks, Apple's Custom Workout feature, Coros Training Hub, or similar platforms, you can create sessions like "10-minute warm-up in Zone 1, 40 minutes in Zone 2, 5-minute cooldown" and sync them straight to your watch.

During the run, your watch displays the current step, the target range, and whether you're above, below, or in the pocket. Many will automatically advance between intervals and alert you when it's time to shift gears.

Heart rate-based intervals, like 4 x 4 minutes in Zone 4 with Zone 1 recovery, where you don't have to do mental math or check the clock.

Progressive long runs that start in Zone 2 and finish in Zone 3.

Hill repeats, where pace is meaningless but effort matters.

Most watches calculate default zones using a generic formula like 220 minus your age, which can be off by 10 to 20 beats for any given individual. If your zones are wrong, your Zone 2 training isn't Zone 2 training.

Here’s how to fix your watch’s heart rate zones:

Find your true max heart rate. The informal way is to just notice what number you see on your watch when you can no longer speak comfortably; the more formal way is this treadmill test. You can also look through your recent hard efforts, like races, hill repeats, or all-out intervals, and see the highest sustained heart rate you've recorded.

Use lactate threshold heart rate instead. Many watches can estimate this automatically after a few hard efforts, and zones built from threshold tend to be more personalized than ones built from max.

Customize the boundaries. Dive into the heart rate zone settings and input your own numbers. Some runners prefer the "MAF" method (180 minus age, with adjustments) for aerobic base building, and most watches let you set that as a custom range.

Recheck every few months. Fitness changes, and so do your zones.

A screen crowded with cadence, vertical oscillation, ground contact time, running power, and lap pace is a recipe for second-guessing.

Create a dedicated Zone 2 data screen with just two or three fields: current heart rate zone, elapsed time, and maybe distance. Turn off auto-scroll so it doesn't flip to a screen full of numbers you don't need. If your watch supports multiple activity profiles, make a separate "Easy Run" profile with this stripped-down layout and keep a different profile for tempo days and races.

A chest strap (or a forearm or upper-arm optical band) is generally more accurate and responsive than the wrist-based sensor on your watch. For heart rate training, where a few beats can mean the difference between Zone 2 and Zone 3, I recommend buying one. This COOSPO heart rate monitor is one of my favorites, and it's only $31.99.

The bottom line: Your smartwatch can make heart rate training far easier, but only if you set it up to support you rather than overwhelm you.

#3446. These Early Black Friday Ring Camera Deals Start at $24.99

If you’re browsing home security options, Ring has one of the best early Black Friday deals that should be on your radar. Right now, you can add an indoor camera and another one at your front door for less than $65. The Ring Indoor Cam 2K is 58% off at $24.99 (originally $59.99), while the Ring Battery Doorbell 2K is 60% off at $39.99 (originally $99.99)—both at their lowest-ever price.

Both offer features like 2K video and two-way talk, but the indoor cam is the simpler purchase if you mainly want to check on a pet or kids and see what’s happening near an entrance. It plugs into an outlet, so there’s no battery to recharge, and its low-light color video helps preserve detail when lights are off or dimmed. However, since it’s a fixed-view camera, keep in mind that you’ll need to position it carefully.

The Battery Doorbell is the better pick if alerting you to visitors, deliveries, and potential intruders is your priority. It has a 140-degree horizontal and vertical field of view that provides head-to-toe framing, plus up to 6x zoom for better detail. You can install it without wiring, though you’ll need to recharge its built-in battery. It also requires a 2.4GHz wifi network.

The main catch with both devices is the ongoing subscription cost: Live viewing, two-way talk, and basic real-time notifications all work without a subscription, but reviewing saved footage requires a paid plan, starting at $4.99 per month or $49.99 annually for one device; coverage for multiple devices at one location starts at $9.99 monthly or $99.99 annually.

At these prices, the Ring Indoor Cam 2K is perfect for occasional live check-ins, while the Ring Battery Doorbell 2K is better suited to monitoring your front entrance. Buying both makes sense if you already have a Ring plan that covers extra devices.

November 2026 is chugging along nicely, and HBO Max is rolling out a fresh wave of titles ready for you to add to your weekend watchlist. True-crime fans can dig a tense limited series that reframes a notorious 2011 murder case as a psychological thriller about a marriage degraded by control and manipulation.

For something equally jaw-dropping but a little more playful, there’s a German documentary chronicling the audacious heist of a 100-kilogram solid-gold coin from a Berlin museum, and the investigation that followed. And if you’d rather sink into something scripted, the acclaimed “City of God: The Fight Rages On” returns for a second season, exploring the power struggles of Rio’s favelas.

That lineup should keep you plenty busy as November continues. Clear your schedule and grab the popcorn, because here are three newly added HBO Max shows you need to add to your watchlist this weekend.

What is it about? This Italian limited series dramatizes one of the most notorious real-life criminal cases in recent Italian history. In 2011, 29-year-old Melania Rea’s body was discovered in a wooded area of the Abruzzo National Park, near the home she shared with her husband and their daughter. It was a murder that gripped the nation and dominated headlines for months. But “Melania Rea” takes you beyond the tabloids to tell the true story behind it, unfolding across parallel timelines to reveal a woman trapped in a marriage that was never quite what it seemed.

Why you should watch it: Across four episodes, the series takes fantastical true crime headlines and transforms them into a psychological thriller about dangerous relationships. It's a great look beneath the surface that brings an often-overlooked situation to light.

What is it about? The sequel series to the 2002 Brazilian film “City of God” returns for a second season, once again exploring the many power struggles of Rio de Janeiro’s favelas. Meanwhile, councilwoman Berenice (Roberta Rodrigues) takes on political corruption, Jerusa (Andréia Horta) hunts down those who destroyed her family, and Leka (Luellem de Castro) turns to funk music and dance parties to try and bring the community together.

Why you should watch it: Filmed on location in Rio de Janeiro and São Paulo, “City of God: The Fight Rages On” matches the energy and storytelling that made its predecessor a classic. Watch "City Of God: The Fight Rages On" season 2 on HBO Max now

What is it about? “Clangold” tells the true story of one of the biggest heists in recent memory. In 2017, thieves stole the “Big Maple Leaf,” a 100-kilogram solid gold Canadian coin worth millions, from Berlin’s Bode Museum. It seemed like the perfect crime, but this German documentary series follows the investigation that followed and proves that it was not. In fact, police were led deep into the city’s notorious organized-crime “clan” underworld in a tense hunt for the culprits, making for this gripping documentary you can watch this weekend.

Why you should watch it: Mixing reenactments with real-world interviews, “Clangold” is much like a real-life thriller. If you love a juicy true crime story with a jaw-dropping hook, you'll tear through this four-episode caper.

#3443. Apple Won't Make a Small Phone so This Company Is Stepping In

Big smartphones have long been the norm. It seems many, if not most, of us prefer our smartphones to be akin to tiny tablets. Even Apple's smallest iPhone isn't that small, with a 6.1-inch display. (Compare that to the 5.4-inch iPhone mini it used to sell.) But just because a lot of us like it that way doesn't mean all of us do.

Despite what companies like Apple would lead you to believe, there are plenty of people out there who want their smartphones to be smaller. For some, the iPhone mini was perfect, featuring a design that most could use comfortably with one hand. While the sales might not have been steady enough for Apple to continue producing the mini line, anecdotally, I know quite a few people who would happily keep using iPhones this small, if only Apple would make more of them. Perhaps you know people like this too; maybe you're one of them.

While the rumor mill does not suggest that Apple plans to make a new iPhone mini, that doesn't mean the dream of the tiny smartphone is dead. Enter "Enough Phone," a new device with a humble goal: to create a "small, modern smartphone that's enough."

Enough Phone really does seem small. The company says its upcoming device is 133mm by 64mm, and less than 12mm thick. That's the equivalent of 5.24 inches by 2.52 inches, and less than 0.47 inches thick. It's remarkably similar to the iPhone 13 mini, at 5.18 by 2.53 inches, and 0.3 inches thick. While the Enough Phone might be a tad larger overall, and perhaps noticeably thicker, it's still reminiscent of that "mini" footprint.

The Enough Phone's 5.3-inch display isn't particularly modern, however. While we don't know the display type, we do know that it has a resolution of 1520 x 720, which may look less sharp to anyone coming from the 2340 x 1080 resolution of the iPhone 13 mini. I'd wager that most people interested in a device like this aren't looking for an ultra-sharp OLED display anyway, but it's worth noting here.

As for the Enough Phone's other specs, the company says it plans to pack in a 2.4GHz MediaTek Dimensity 7500 chip with 8GB of RAM, 128GB of built-in storage, though you can expand that with a microSD card (something you don't see on many smartphones these days). The current plan is to ship with a single 50MP Sony IMX766 rear camera, and a 32MP selfie cam, which would be amongst the highest-resolution front-facing cameras on any smartphone. It supports 5G, Wi-Fi 6, and eSIM, with the option to use a physical SIM as well.

Enough is also aiming to make its smartphone more repairable than the competition. While smartphone OEMs have made slight improvements to repairability in recent years, few phones are made to be opened up by the user, and their components replaced. While Enough Phone isn't fully modular, it is designed with easy-to-open screws, and comes with a fully replaceable 3,500 mAh battery. Combined with promised software support through 2032, Enough says this device "should last you into the next decade."

Now, all of these specs are targets, as the phone is currently in the prototype stage. Enough says that final details may change "slightly" during testing. I would at least hope that the dimensions, particularly the screen size, remain the same by launch. What will likely stay the same, however, are the ringtones: Enough says they hired composer Brian Squillance of LAANDS to produce the jingles for its phone, which is a neat touch.

Unfortunately for Apple fans, however, Enough Phone isn't an iPhone. That said, it doesn't have to be an Android phone, either. While you can buy the phone with Android 17 installed, you can also choose to run OdysseyOS, a minimalist "de-Googled" operating system made by SLEKE. Enough says OdysseyOS is meant for "intentional phone use," which might appeal to anyone looking for a phone that's "dumb" as well as small.

Of course, neither operating system is iOS. Unfortunately for Apple users, the only true iPhone options here are to continue using an old iPhone mini, which Apple does still support, or to opt for an iPhone 17e, the smallest iPhone the company currently makes. It's pretty easy to find a used and refurbished iPhone 13 mini for reasonable price; but while they can still run the latest version of iOS, you won't be able to take advantage of all of Apple's newest features. Plus, while there's no telling how long Apple plans to support the 13 line for, it won't support it forever—by iOS 28 or iOS 29, your phone might lose support entirely.

If the promise of a modern mini smartphone entices you, you can back the Enough Phone on Kickstarter today. While the company's $399 "Super Early Bird" reward is already sold out, as of this article, the "Early Bird" reward is still up. That reward costs $449, and includes a glass screen protector pre-installed, a protective case, a USB-C cable, a USB-C to 3.5mm headphone adapter, a hex screwdriver, and green "Founders' Edition" backplate screws. Enough says that the retail price for its phone will be $599 after the campaign, so you can save $150 by backing the phone today—if you're serious about small phones. The Enough Phone is slated for a May 2027 launch.

#3441. 'Hunger Games' Books Officially Top 100 Million Ahead of New Movie

The odds, after all this time, after all 18 years, are ever in our favor because, in the almost two decades since Suzanne Collins introduced readers to Katniss Everdeen, Panem is as popular as ever. What began as a dystopian novel about teenagers forced to fight to the death has grown into one of the biggest young adult franchises in publishing history, spawning blockbuster movies, bestselling prequels, and a whole lot of memorable performances. And wouldn't you know it? The series is, remarkably, still breaking records at an almost unbelievable rate.

Scholastic has confirmed that The Hunger Games book series has surpassed 100 million copies worldwide across its five novels, ahead of the November 20 theatrical release of The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping. The figure includes print and digital editions, cementing the franchise's status as one of the most successful young adult book series ever published.

That milestone includes all five books, starting with the original three of The Hunger Games, Catching Fire, and Mockingjay, alongside the prequels The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes and Sunrise on the Reaping. Reaping has been a massive success, too, and it's sold more than 4.4 million English-language copies across six major markets by January 2026, including over 3.3 million in the United States alone. It also sold more than 1.5 million copies during its first week.

The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping will revisit the world of Panem 24 years before the events of The Hunger Games, starting on the morning of the reaping of the 50th Hunger Games, also known as the Second Quarter Quell.

The film stars Joseph Zada (Invisible Boys) as Haymitch Abernathy, Ralph Fiennes (Schindler's List) as President Snow, Elle Fanning (The Great) as Effie Trinket, Kieran Culkin (Succession) as Caesar Flickerman, Jesse Plemons (Civil War) as Plutarch Heavensbee, Whitney Peak (Gossip Girl) as Lenore Dove Baird, Josh Hutcherson (Zathura) as Peeta Mellark, Woody Harrelson (Kingpin) as Older Haymitch Abernathy and Jennifer Lawrence (Red Sparrow) as Katniss Everdeen.

The Hunger Games novels are available in print, ebook, and audiobook formats. The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping opens in theaters November 20, 2026. #3437. MagSafe Monday: Pelican’s MagSafe wallet is built for the people who still carry cash

I’ve been on a Pelican kick this fall. It started with the Pelican MagSafe Wallet, then the Pelican MagSafe Battery Pack, and the reason is pretty simple: once the weather turns cool, I want iPhone accessories built for the outdoors because I am outside more. The Pelican Protector Magnetic Money Clip Wallet is really helpful is you want something rugged, but also supports holding cash.

MagSafe Monday: Every Monday, Bradley Chambers looks at the latest and greatest in the MagSafe and wireless charging industry to help you get the most out of your Apple devices that support wireless charging.

Most magnetic wallets are a simple card sleeve and nothing else. If you carry a few $5 bills for tips, cash-only places, etc., you end up folding them around a card and hoping they don’t slip out. The Pelican Protector Magnetic Money Clip Wallet has a stainless steel money clip on the outside of the wallet, so the cash rides on the back, where you can access it without pulling your credit cards out. It’s the same hard-shell construction as the rest of Pelican’s lineup, with the same MagSafe magnets.

The wallet holds up to five cards, which is just about perfect for my use cases. That covers my Driver’s license, debit card, and a few credit cards. There are ridges inside that push the cards up when you squeeze, so you’re not digging with your nails. A steel plate blocks RFID scanning, and the shell is rated IPX4 for water, which covers rain, etc.

Pelican calls its drop protection military-grade, which is what every accessory company says. A more useful way to think about it is that it’s a hard-shell wallet rather than a leather or silicone one.

Two things to know going in with this wallet. Five cards plus a clip of cash makes for a thick back on your phone, so this isn’t a very slim wallet. If you’re replacing a money clip, you are basically combining the two into one.

If you never carry much cash, the original Pelican wallet is the better pick. If you do want to carry a bunch of cash, the Pelican Protector Magnetic Money Clip Wallet is an awesome pickup.

The Pelican Protector Magnetic Money Clip Wallet is available on Amazon and directly from Pelican.

#3436. Three Ways to Avoid CAPTCHA Prompts When Using a VPN

VPNs make it harder to track your online activity across websites, but it also makes them suspicious about your origins. When you borrow an IP address that hundreds of other people are also using for any number of reasons, you’re much more likely to get repeat verification requests from online firewalls.

CAPTCHAs are simple puzzles that websites use to filter out bots and spam. They’re supposed to be easy for people but hard for robots, such as simple object recognition tasks or audio-visual challenges. However, they can still disrupt your browsing experience if they happen too frequently.

Most modern CAPTCHA providers, like Google's reCAPTCHA v3 or Cloudflare Turnstile, start working long before they give you a puzzle to solve. It usually starts with a risk score that studies your IP address, browser and device signals, or recent online activity.

If the CAPTCHA provider can’t confidently identify your request as human based on those signals, it requests that you complete a puzzle before deciding if the request should be blocked. That means when you get repeat CAPTCHA requests, there’s something affecting your browser’s risk score. For example, popular VPN servers spread the same IP address across any number of users, which can easily make a website mistake you for a bot farm. If you change your IP address frequently by switching servers often, that might look suspicious too.

Luckily, there are ways to deal with frequent CAPTCHA requests using tools and services available with your browser and VPN. Cloudflare has already cut its CAPTCHA requests by 91% using its Managed Challenge platform. Apple has also been shipping token-based verification on devices since iOS 16 and macOS Ventura. In June 2026, Cloudflare even announced a joint effort called the Private Access Control Tokens (PACT) standard with Chrome, Edge, Firefox, and Shopify.

While there’s no direct off switch for CAPTCHAs, you can use different fixes to improve your browser’s trust signals when using the internet. That way, you’re less likely to be hounded by verification requests.

The easiest fix for repeat CAPTCHAs is to stop connecting to whichever server your VPN app picks automatically. Proton recommends choosing servers with lower traffic load. In fact, its apps display load as a percentage to help you avoid the most crowded options. I'd also skip big traffic hubs like New York or London, since that's where most traffic originates from. Servers in smaller cities located nearby are often just as fast but never as populated.

You should also avoid changing IP addresses too frequently, which can look suspicious on its own. Pick a server that seems to behave well, then continue using it for at least one session. Also remember you’re more likely to get premium server options if you’re on a paid VPN plan. Major platforms like ExpressVPN, Surfshark, Proton, and Nord are particularly likely to have a larger server collection to pick from.

Costs nothing more than your current subscription

Hopping between servers often can backfire

Private Access Tokens (PAT) let you verify the authenticity of your request using your device rather than an IP address. Apple calls it Automatic Verification, where an Apple server validates your device and Apple Account to assign you an anonymous token.

To enable Automatic Verification on an iPhone or iPad, go to Settings > [your name] > Sign-In & Security > Automatic Verification. On a Mac, open System Settings > [your name] > Sign-In & Security > Automatic Verification.

Unfortunately, there’s no equivalent feature for Windows, Android, and Linux users. That said, Cloudflare offers the Silk extension for Chrome, Firefox, and Edge that serves a similar function. A quick look at the ratings will tell you it’s not as effective, but Cloudflare’s upcoming cross-browser standard called PACT seems promising once it is released.

Doesn’t share personal details with websites

Chrome and Firefox extensions can be unreliable

If you pay a bit extra for a dedicated IP add-on, VPN providers can assign you a unique IP address that isn’t shared with anyone else. For example, NordVPN offers dedicated IPs in 30 countries for $2-5 a month and Surfshark charges $3.75 a month for it.

There are also dedicated providers like Private Internet Access, which charges $3.99 per month for a zero-trust setup so not even their employees know which IP address is assigned to you. On the other hand, Proton VPN offers dedicated IPs only to business plan users, so you’ll need to be on the Workspace Standard, Premium, or Enterprise plans to get one.

That said, there is a trade-off here too. NordVPN itself admits that a dedicated IP makes it easier to link online activity back to a single user. Also, many websites can still tell that the IP address originated from a VPN data center rather than a consumer’s device.

Get unique IP addresses with pristine reputation

Works across desktop, mobile, and even smart TVs

Also functions as an allowlisted address for work

Add-ons cost more on top of the VPN subscription

Offers less anonymity than shared VPN servers

#3435. iOS 27.3: Three new iPhone features coming soon

iOS 27.3 is currently in beta and packed with new features, here are three that will hit your iPhone when the update launches next month.

Apple Health is getting some big changes in iOS 27.3 for all Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhones.

The new Health app adds Insights and Longevity tabs that provide personalized and intelligent recommendations related to your health. New features include educational videos featuring clinical experts, at-home movement evaluations using your iPhone’s camera, the ability to order and log labs, and a lot more.

Apple originally tested the new Health app in the iOS 27.2 beta, but it was removed before the public launch. The company said from the start, though, that the app would return and ship later this year, now confirmed with iOS 27.3.

Apple Music adds a new ‘Selfie Sing’ feature in iOS 27.3 that’s clearly designed to be used on social platforms like TikTok.

Selfie Sing lets you create karaoke videos of yourself using the iPhone’s camera and Apple Music’s built-in lyrics feature. As seen above, the feature puts lyrics onscreen below your camera feed so you can sing along to your favorite songs then share your video on social.

It won’t be for everyone, but Selfie Sing is a fun addition that represents one of Apple’s few attempts at a social-centric offering.

When iPhone Duo launched, it included a variety of exclusive features related to StandBy mode. But with iOS 27.3, Apple is bringing these StandBy improvements to all iPhones.

Additionally, iOS 27.3 lets you create multiple versions of each face for easily swiping between them. These features won’t be new for iPhone Duo users, but it’s great to see Apple bring them to more iPhone models.

Which iOS 27.3 features are you most excited about? Let us know in the comments.

We're deep into November, and the sofa is just screaming for some quality screen time. Fortunately, the best new movies and shows to watch this weekend bring everything from Middle-earth magic to psychological horror and star-powered action to Netflix, Prime Video, Peacock and other streaming services, as well as theaters and broadcast TV.

As Tom's Guide's streaming editor, I've rounded up and ranked this week's biggest releases to help you cut out scroll time. "The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power" returns for season 3, while Jessica Chastain pulls double duty with the unsettling "Other Mommy" and the country music thriller "Heartland." Brad Pitt brings the star power to "Heart of the Beast," and "12 12 12" and "The Good Daughter" offer even more reasons to keep the remote handy.

So grab a blanket, raid the snack stash and put those holiday shopping errands on hold for a little longer. Here's what to watch this weekend, ranked by must-watch factor.

Kelly recently reviewed "Black Doves" season 2 and "The Gilded Age" season 4.

Genre: Heist thrillerAvailable now: 2 episodes (about 50 min each)What it's about: A bank vault buried beneath Zurich is about to have a very bad day. Anthony Mackie stars as a disgraced FBI agent hunting Jamie Dornan's career criminal across Europe in a high-stakes game of cat and mouse. The twist? The story unfolds across three timelines: the 12 months leading up to the robbery, the 12 hours of the job itself and the 12 days that follow.Why it's worth your time: The show's nonlinear structure gives this high-stakes caper more moving parts than your average smash-and-grab. With a sprawling European chase, a massive payday and a personal grudge in the mix, there's plenty to keep the adrenaline pumping.Where to watch: Apple TV

Genre: Crime thrillerAvailable now: All 6 episodes (about 50 min each)What it's about: Two decades after a brutal attack shattered their family, sisters Charlotte (Meghann Fahy) and Samantha Quinn (Rose Byrne) are still picking up the pieces. When a similar crime rocks their Georgia hometown, the sisters reunite to help investigate. But solving the case means digging up family secrets that were never meant to see daylight.Why it's worth your time: Byrne and Fahy make a compelling sister act, bringing plenty of heart and prickliness to this Karin Slaughter adaptation. With Brendan Gleeson in the mix and a small-town mystery at its center, there's plenty to keep thriller fans hooked.Where to watch: Peacock

Genre: Comedy-dramaRuntime: 1 hr 43 minWhat it’s about: Once an award-winning actress, Misty Green (Rosalind Eleazar) is now scrambling to revive her career, dodge a string of personal disasters and find a new place to live. With just seven days before she's evicted, she reconnects with her former agent (Topher Grace) and crosses paths with a colorful cast of Hollywood misfits, including a troubled brother (Daniel Kaluuya) and a shady filmmaker (Adam Driver).Why you should watch: Chris Rock writes, directs and co-stars in this sharp-edged look at Hollywood's transactional relationships, racial and economic inequities, and the perils of letting ego get in the way of a comeback. Eleazar (“Slow Horses”) is a magnetic mess as Misty, bringing emotional depth to a character who isn't always easy to root for. Where to watch: Netflix

Genre: Fantasy adventure dramaAvailable now: 4 episodes (about 50 min each)What it's about: Middle-earth is in deep trouble. Five years after Sauron (Charlie Vickers) sent the Elves packing, the Dark Lord is plotting world domination, with just one thing standing between him and total victory: a very tricky piece of jewelry. As he struggles to forge the One Ring, Galadriel (Morfydd Clark), Elrond (Robert Aramayo) and the other free peoples must unite before it's too late.Why it's worth your time: The stakes are bigger, the battles bloodier and Sauron's ego remains absolutely astronomical. Celeborn (Jamie Campbell Bower) enters the picture, giving Galadriel a rather inconvenient husband problem. Tolkien fans, your watch has begun.Where to watch: Prime Video

Sign up to the weekly Tom's Streaming Guide to stay in the loop with the latest releases and top recommendations across your favorite streaming services. We’ve got you covered with a complete guide on what’s worth watching.

Genre: Mystery thrillerRuntime: 1 hr 52 minWhat it’s about: Jessica Chastain stars as Misty Jones, a retired country music superstar who returns to Nashville after 20 years away to find her missing niece, Charlie (real-life country singer Carter Faith). But the search takes Misty into the city's darker corners, where old secrets, shady suspects and a few familiar faces make it clear that Music City has a sinister side.Why you should watch: Think “Country Strong” meets film noir, with a little murder-mystery twang. Chastain gets to play a deliciously prickly former queen of country who isn't afraid to ruffle feathers (or throw punches). It features original music from Chastain and Faith, plus a supporting cast that includes Garrett Hedlund, Ross Lynch and Jennifer Nettles.Where to watch: Netflix

Genre: Biographical dramaRuntime: 2 hrs 7 minWhat it’s about: In 1977, disability rights activist Judy Heumann (Ruth Madeley) and a coalition of fed-up protesters occupy a San Francisco federal building for 28 days, demanding the government enforce their civil rights under Section 504. Mark Ruffalo plays the bureaucrat they're up against, while Dylan O'Brien is a reporter who gets an up-close look at the fight.Why you should watch: Siân Heder (“CODA”) directs this true story of a group of people who were told to wait their turn and decided they'd waited long enough. Turns out, sometimes the only way to get a seat at the table is to take over the whole damn building.Where to watch: Apple TV

Genre: DocumentaryRuntime: 1 hr 44 minWhat it’s about: Richard Avedon didn't just photograph the 20th century; he helped define its look. In this documentary, director Ron Howard explores the life and legacy of the groundbreaking photographer, from his iconic fashion shoots and celebrity portraits to his unflinching images of civil rights activists and everyday Americans. With never-before-seen photos, archival footage and interviews with those closest to him, “Avedon” gets behind the lens to examine the complicated man behind the camera.Why you should watch: Even if you know nothing about photography, Avedon's influence is hard to miss. Interviews with the likes of Isabella Rossellini, Twiggy, Lauren Hutton and Calvin Klein offer a personal look at the artist, while his impressive archive makes this a feast for the eyes.Where to watch: Netflix

Genre: Survival thrillerRuntime: 1 hr 41 minWhat it’s about: Brad Pitt stars as James Belmont, a retired Special Forces veteran whose Alaskan wilderness getaway goes wrong when his seaplane crashes, leaving him stranded 58 miles from civilization. With only his combat-trained German Shepherd, Odin, by his side, James must battle brutal terrain, dangerous wildlife and his own injuries to make it back alive.Why you should watch: Pitt and a heroic German Shepherd battling the Alaskan wilderness? That's an irresistible movie pitch. Director David Ayer (“Fury”) delivers some tense survival sequences, and Odin is an undeniable scene-stealer.Where to watch: Prime Video (with purchase)

Genre: Historical romantic dramaAvailable now: 6 episodes (about 50 min each)What it's about: The final chapter of Elisabeth's (Devrim Lingnau) imperial saga finds her marriage to Franz (Philip Froissant) on shaky ground after a devastating war and his infidelity. Seeking refuge abroad, she encounters Hungarian revolutionary Count Andrássy (Dejan Bućin), while Franz's brother Maximilian (Johannes Nussbaum) sets his sights on Mexico's throne. #3433. ‘The Chosen’ Season 6 Puts Jesus on Trial in Prime Video’s Historical Epic | Review

Since its first season dropped in 2019, The Chosen has become a global phenomenon. Before this, the story of Jesus Christ (played here by Jonathan Roumie) and his disciples had not been told in a long-form, multi-season television format. Sure, there were miniseries and theatrical renditions, but nothing aimed to go so in depth in exploring the life of those who followed Christ. For five seasons, the series — which began on VidAngel and has grown into a Prime Video hit — has gone beyond the biblical text, for better or worse, to bring first-century Judea to life for modern viewers. With Season 6, premiering on November 15, the entire narrative reaches its long-anticipated climax.

In the fifth season, dubbed The Chosen: Last Supper (which earned a near-perfect audience score), Jesus and his disciples sit down for their final meal before his death. Unpacking the events from the latter chapters of the New Testament accounts, the season covers Christ's arrival in Jerusalem leading up to Judas Iscariot's (Luke Dimyan) fated betrayal in the Garden of Gethsemane. Thus, Season 6 picks up right where we left off. Judas arrives with the Jewish religious leaders and the temple guard to bring Jesus in, representing the fallout from previous seasons. From there, Jesus' arrest starts a wildfire throughout Jerusalem, as his followers are divided, torn between following their rabbi's teachings or going to war on behalf of their Messiah. It's in this distress that the season resides, taking place across a single morning, from daybreak to just before the "third hour of the day" (around 9 AM).

If previous seasons succeeded in balancing the struggle between personal tribulation and the light that comes from Jesus' words, Season 6 revels largely in the former. While there are undoubtedly moments where faith and love prevail, it's only through many tears, deep sorrow, and excruciating pain — emotionally for most, physically for Jesus. Indeed, The Chosen begins its penultimate season with a disclaimer that graphic scenes of torture, violence, and even suicide will be depicted throughout. No, this isn't a TV version of The Passion of the Christ, though any similarities between them are unavoidable. Creator Dallas Jenkins and company never quite get as gory as Mel Gibson. Some may see this as wisdom (and consideration) for the show's audience, while others may feel it doesn't go far enough in representing the brutality of Roman torture. I'm willing to give them the benefit of the doubt, as anything The Chosen leaves to the imagination can be easily pictured in the mind's eye.

Roumie's performance this season is far more understated than before. In the Gospel accounts, Jesus famously had very little to say between his arrest and the cross, and that largely remains true here — with some thematic exceptions. Indeed, there is one moment in the sixth episode (and the final chapter to be released in 2026) that feels a bit unbelievable given what Jesus has endured, but, otherwise, Jenkins does well to keep most of his verbal efforts brief. After all, the time for words has passed. Jesus is finally at the event that the entire series has built towards, and so his focus is fixed on the task at hand. This, of course, leads to some interesting reactions from those around him, namely the authorities who claim to hold his life in their hands. Yet, as he famously tells Pontius Pilate (Andrew James Allen) in the Gospel of John, "You would have no power over me if it were not given to you from above."

While Christ himself is the catalyst for the pre-Passover disruptions in Jerusalem, The Chosen's supporting cast anchors the season. As the disciples go into hiding, the Sanhedrin convenes in secret under the oversight of the high priest Caiaphas (Richard Fancy) to bring Jesus' claims to light. The vitriol and contempt with which they view the Nazarene explodes through the screen, but, unfortunately for the Pharisaical elites, they do not have the authority to put him to death — only Rome does. The Chosen continues to explore the tension within the Sanhedrin itself, represented in Caiaphas and Nicodemus (Erick Avari). The show thoroughly details their respective (though differing) motivations for examining Christ, pulling from both historical and biblical texts to bring these ancient figures to life. Avari is a genuine on-screen delight this year, once more getting his due after such an extended on-screen absence (he has been gone since Season 1, though returned briefly last season).

Yet, The Chosen explores more than just Jesus' Jewish persecutors. Perhaps where Season 6 thrives most is in unpacking the various trials of Christ by those given authority by Rome. Characters like Herod Antipas (Paul Ben-Victor) and Pontius Pilate are heavily utilized this season, hoping to retain their power and keep the peace by pushing the apparent "King of the Jews" back on the other. Ben-Victor's concentrated presence as Herod adds an uncomfortable levity to the events, making a mockery of Jesus in the midst of his suffering. Pilate, on the other hand, is a more finely tuned figure. Although I thought Andrew James Allen to be a strange cast at first — he infuses the Roman prefect with an almost boyish charisma — his portrayal here fits in quite well with the show's penchant for reinventing such notable historical and religious figures.

Of course, those affected by Jesus' arrest the most are those within his own circle. Simon Peter (Shahar Isaac) and John (George H. Xanthis) follow Christ at a distance while the remaining disciples, led by Big James (Abe Bueno Jallad) (and sans Judas), go into hiding to evade capture, unraveling amongst themselves. The way the series explores the debate among them — as they wonder how they should proceed — is deeply engaging. The show offers a genuine level of frustration and turmoil that most portrayals don't touch on. Even within Peter and John, uncertainty rules every action and thought, though both hot-headed followers have clearly come far in the last few years under Christ's tutelage. As in the Gospel accounts, this prompts the women, namely Mary of Nazareth (Vanessa Benavente) and Mary Magdalene (Elizabeth Tabish), to follow closely after Jesus. Season 6 gives viewers a powerful glimpse at how Mary would react to her son's arrest, torture, and death sentence. Benavente embodies a parental heartbreak that's equal parts human and profound.

Of course, not every creative choice works. The Chosen experienced some understandable pushback ahead of the premiere when dropping a clip from the teaser that portrays the angelic heavenly host as warriors from differing human cultures. While there's no reason that angels can't appear as different races (indeed, it makes sense that they would), the choice to dress them in historical human garb rather than some unified heavenly armor was both odd and somewhat unsettling. It just takes the viewer out of it. But the biggest departure from the biblical text is Judas himself. The Chosen has done its best to portray Judas as a character and not a caricature, and that is to be celebrated. But while the Gospel accounts paint his portrayal based solely on human greed (and the literal influence of Satan), Season 6 hardly touches on this at all. Instead, these episodes subvert what we know about Judas by suggesting that he betrayed Jesus not simply for his own sinful gain, but because he wanted to force Christ's messianic hand — the money was just a bonus.

It's not uncommon for The Chosen to reframe some of the most pivotal biblical moments when bringing them to the screen. Sometimes, going beyond the text helps to emphasize the point of the text and flesh out the characters; other times it comes across as unbelievable or disingenuous. The Judas revisions are the latter. This isn't the only moment that may give viewers pause this season, either. There is some disruption among the disciples in the later episodes that likewise feels more like an attempt to generate on-screen drama than a natural progression of where we know the story is headed. Perhaps to some viewers this isn't a problem — and some of this is, no doubt, in the eye of this beholder — but when spending a whole season already prolonging a relatively straightforward text (and doing it quite well, in most regards), the "drama for drama's sake" moments stick out like a sore thumb.

What may come as the biggest shock to those tuning in expecting to see the crucifixion is that these first six episodes lead up to the event but don't actually show it. This isn't to say that The Chosen intends to skip the most important moment in the entire Bible, but that the show will go on hiatus for several months between early December and March, culminating in a feature-length finale: The Chosen Crucifixion. Unlike the rest of this season, which was filmed largely in Texas and Utah, the upcoming crucifixion scenes were filmed, like The Passion before it, in Matera, Italy. That said, the last episode of the sixth season to drop this year concludes with the cross in full view, and we all know what will happen next.

The Chosen Season 6 premieres November 15 on Prime Video, while the finale, The Chosen Crucifixion, will premiere in theaters on March 12, 2027.

The Chosen Season 6 expands on the trial of Christ like never before.
