#3431. Apple to open new Developer Center in Istanbul as part of broader Turkey investment

Apple today announced a long-term investment in Turkey, with seven new facilities focused on app development and manufacturing set to open in the country starting next year. Here are the details.

In a press release issued on its Turkish Newsroom (via MacRumors), Apple today announced a series of long-term investments in Turkey.

The announcement comes as former CEO and current executive chairman Tim Cook visits the country, as he’s been sharing on X.

Merhaba Istanbul! What a stunning view from the Grand Bazaar this morning alongside talented creator Cem Başak. Thrilled to visit this remarkable country! pic.twitter.com/c4daBBXe1l

The company’s investment in Turkey will be three-pronged, with the opening of five new Apple Developer Academies, one Apple Developer Center, and one Apple Manufacturing Academy.

Apple says it will open five new developer academies across Turkey over the next three years, with the first opening in Istanbul in 2027, alongside its new developer center. The Apple Manufacturing Academy, meanwhile, is set to open in Ankara in 2028.

Here’s Cook commenting on today’s announcement (translation ours):

“Apple has been serving our customers and communities in Turkey for 35 years. With this new commitment, we are proud to support the next generation of innovative entrepreneurs in the years ahead. […] Turkey’s developer community is developing apps used around the world. Meanwhile, small and medium-sized businesses stand out as organizations creating opportunities throughout the country. This investment provides developers and businesses with access to the training and resources they need to take their brightest ideas even further, as well as to Apple experts.”

Apple explained that its developer academies will offer “free, intensive nine-month programs focused on coding, design, marketing, project management, and artificial intelligence technologies,” while the developer center “will provide developers, entrepreneurs, and start-ups with a hands-on learning experience by providing access to the latest tools, technologies, and resources, as well as Apple experts and events.”

As for its manufacturing academy in Ankara, which will mark the company’s first Apple Manufacturing Academy outside the US, it will “provide free training and consultancy to small and medium-sized businesses, students and innovative entrepreneurs.”

Led by Apple experts, the curriculum will help participants adopt AI and intelligent manufacturing techniques through courses on machine learning technology, predictive maintenance, advanced automation, and robotics, as well as interactive workshops on lean operations and production efficiency.

Apple's new ceramic watch cases are mighty pretty

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Should you upgrade to the new ceramic Apple Watch 12? It’s been quite a while since Apple offered its flagship wearable in a material other than metal. The last ceramic Apple Watch model was 2019’s Series 5.

Long a fan of the ceramic case, I was thrilled to see Apple bring it back for 2026. That excitement only increased after my colleague Jane got her hands on the Series 12 Ceramic at Apple HQ and confirmed its immense beauty.

But is the Apple Watch 12 Ceramic right for you? I can think of three major reasons that justify the upgrade, along with two drawbacks worth considering.

The Apple Watch Series 12 comes in ceramic for the first time since 2019. Compared to Apple's metal case options, ceramic is more durable, with a smooth, pearl-like finish. Choose from Midnight Blue or Pearl White.

Beauty is in the eyes — on the wrist — of the beholder. Let’s be real, though: The primary reason most folks are considering the Apple Watch 12 in a ceramic case is because of its premium and unique look and feel.

The Series 12 is offered in both Pearl White and Night Blue ceramic options; I’m particularly partial to the former, which apparently looks a bit more cream than white IRL with a lovely pearl-like finish.

The Night Blue option, meanwhile, is more of a muted, metallic blue, giving it a less ceramic-like look than the white one. It’s also overall a bit more subtle on the wrist, i.e., less likely to lead to folks "ooing" and "aahing" at parties.

Apple’s ceramic cases are also smoother to the touch than the metal options, adding to the premium vibes.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

In addition to a more premium look and feel, the ceramic Apple Watch 12 models are also more durable than their metal counterparts. Apple’s ceramic case combines zirconium dioxide and aluminum oxide, which results in exceptional hardness/scratch resistance, fade resistance, and structural strength.

Ceramic is also more skin-friendly than aluminum or titanium, something worth considering if you have sensitive skin.

For the standard Apple Watch 12 aluminum models, users can choose between a more affordable GPS-only watch or a slightly pricier GPS+cellular model. The Series 12 Ceramic, on the other hand, only comes with both GPS and cellular, saving you the decision.

Better yet, unlike aluminum or titanium, ceramic doesn’t tend to block cellular and WiFi signals. Now, Apple won’t tell you the connectivity of the ceramic models is superior to that of the metal ones thanks to this higher degree of radio transparency, but I suspect it is.

The primary reason to skip the ceramic Apple Watch Series 12 is the cost. The standard aluminum Series 12 starts at $399 for the 42mm GPS option. The titanium Series 12 starts at $699, while the ceramic Series 12 will set you back either a cool $899 for the 42mm or a piggy-bank-smashing $949 for the 46mm.

Those prices make the Ceramic Series 12 even more expensive than the Apple Watch Ultra 4.

The other reason to consider skipping the Apple Watch 12 in ceramic is its comparably larger size and weight versus the aluminum and titanium models. For example, the 46mm Midnight Blue option weighs 52.9 g compared to 38.6 g for the aluminum 46mm.

The ceramic model is also 1 mm taller and 1 mm wider than the aluminum models, making the bezel appear slightly chunkier. Finally, the Series 12 Ceramic is 0.15 mm thicker, though I’m not certain you’ll notice that increase.

#3426. I Played Wendy's RPG, and It's Actually Worth It for the Free Food

November is a huge month for video games. Nintendo dropped its remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time for the Switch 2 last week, and the long-awaited Grand Theft Auto VI is right around the corner. But the game we've been waiting for most of all also launched this month: WendyQuest, the free RPG from Wendy's. (No, this is not a joke.)

Despite the absurdity of a hamburger chain making a full video game (complete with Wendy's-themed puns), the thing is, this game is pretty solid—even if it is a promotion at the end of the day. WendyQuest's main purpose is to offer customers coupons they can use toward purchases in real life, though it's a bit of a commitment. It took me just under an hour of gameplay before I earned my first coupon, and Wendy's says it takes roughly 15 hours to beat. All that to say, this is a pretty unique marketing campaign.

I was surprised booting up WendyQuest on my iPhone. This doesn't necessarily feel like a thrown-together product. On the flip side, the production quality is quite high. The music is solid and very much traditionally RPG; there are even three save slots, in case you plan to return to this RPG again and again.

There's even a story, albeit cheesy (no pun intended): As the game explains, the "Four Great Spirits of Flavor" created Savoria, "a food-rich paradise." All was well until Mech Corp, led by the evil Dr. MechBorg, built robots to take over Savoria. The plot is far from compelling, and the writing can be a little over the top, but hey, I'll give them credit: They thought through a full story here.

You play as Wendy, the "representation of true culinary excellence and taste as dictated by the four ancient spirits of flavor." Wendy (or The Wendy, as some call her) is tasked with saving the world, traveling between villages and picking up new characters along the way. The game world even has "real" Wendy's locations you can visit. These act like inns and shops in other RPGs, giving you a chance to heal while also buying equipment.

Like other RPGs, WendyQuest uses turn-based combat. You have to charge up your attacks, but stop before they hit 100%, or you'll miss. (It took me a while to master the timing.) I'm pretty impressed with how challenging some of these battles can be, though you are quickly given the option of an amulet that gives you a huge leg-up in combat. You don't have to take it, but it makes fights easier if you're only in it for the coupons. That, combined with the spatulas the game encourages you to buy, lets you mow down enemies. You can also utilize your companions here: "Frygor," for example, can either attack enemies with a barrage of fries, or use those fries to build a shield to protect you.

While there are tons of enemies to fight, the key baddies are the "mechs." There are five in total, and after you defeat each, you get a coupon. Spoiler alert: The first mech drops the "Fry Stone," which nets you a coupon for a free order of medium fries—though you need to buy something in tandem, as well as use the Wendy's app. While I stopped my gaming here for this article, the other four coupons are:

Free biscuit or croissant (I didn't even know Wendy's sold biscuits and croissants)

Again, it's wild that WendyQuest has a 10+ hour campaign, with over 1,000 lines of dialogue to boot. I'm not sure this is a game I'm going to see through to the end, but I'll admit, it's a fun marketing approach from Wendy's. Sure, they could have run a promotion in the Wendy's app to give people coupons, but instead, they built an entire RPG. I respect it. You can download the game for iOS, Android, or Steam.

#3421. Report: Apple saved over $5 billion in taxes through Singapore and Ireland in 2026

A new Financial Times report reveals how Apple saved billions in taxes in 2026 by shifting profits through Singapore and Ireland. Here are the details.

A few days ago, Apple published its annual Form 10-K, as required by the SEC, containing detailed information about its financial performance and operations for its 2026 fiscal year.

Included in the form, as the FT noted, is information regarding how Apple reduced its tax bill by billions of dollars through its operations in Singapore and Ireland.

For years, Apple’s tax arrangements in Ireland were the subject of scrutiny, culminating in a 2024 ruling by the EU’s top court that required the company to pay €13 billion in back taxes. Apple completed the payment in 2025.

That came a few years after Apple announced plans to bring most of its $252 billion in overseas cash back to the US, following tax reforms introduced during Donald Trump’s first administration.

Since then, to discourage companies from shifting profits to countries with lower tax rates, more than 130 countries have agreed to introduce a minimum corporate tax rate of 15% for large multinational companies, as part of a 2021 initiative coordinated by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD).

Under the agreement, companies that pay less than 15% in a particular country may face additional taxes to make up the difference. The new rules also resulted in an additional $2.5 billion in taxes for Apple in Singapore in 2026, according to the company’s SEC filing.

Ireland adopted the new rules in 2024, followed by Singapore in 2025.

Back to the FT’s report, it notes that new US accounting rules now require publicly traded companies to disclose when their taxes on overseas profits differ significantly from the 21% US federal corporate tax rate.

These new requirements revealed that Apple saved $2.7 billion in taxes through Singapore in 2026, surpassing the $2.6 billion it saved through Ireland.

If Apple had been taxed on all of its global profits in 2026 at the US federal rate, it would have incurred a total bill of $33bn — demonstrating the scale of the $5bn tax reduction it received from booking profits in Ireland and Singapore. The company incurred corporation taxes totalling $27bn this year.

The FT also noted that Apple’s effective tax rate in Singapore fluctuated around 10% between 2023 and 2025, but is expected to approach 15% under the new rules. Singapore’s standard corporate tax rate is 17%.

Black Friday discounts may not be quite as exciting as they used to be, but it doesn't change the fact that it's the perfect time of year to buy a brand new smartphone. Pulling the trigger at launch often feels like being ripped off, and Black Friday is one of the few times we get to enjoy some serious discounts.

Considering how much phone prices have risen this year, with no sign of stopping, saving some money is more important than ever. But it's not quite as simple as loading up Amazon on November 27 and looking for a new deal. There are plenty of ways to maximize your savings both on Black Friday, and the run up to the day itself.

So, to help you out, here are seven essential tips to save money on your new phone this Black Friday.

The most obvious thing to remember is that you shouldn't stick to a specific retailer or carrier to get your phone. If you want to get the best deal you'll need to shop around, and see where your chosen smartphone is on sale and how much everyone is selling it for. Only then can you actually figure out the best place to actually buy it.

But always remember that you should always look at the full scope of the deals, rather than just the listed price or monthly payment.

If you prefer to buy a phone through a carrier, and pay off the price over two to four years, then you'll likely gravitate towards the mobile carriers' own stores. But you should always remember to check out MVNOs as well.

MVNOs may be virtual operators that piggyback off the infrastructure of the big three, but that doesn't mean they don't sell phones too. In fact some of them have a habit of offering competitive prices to try and pique your interest. Mint Mobile is a good example of this, but there are a bunch of other MVNOs to choose from — some operated by the main carriers, and others than are independent.

Sign up to the Tom's iGuide weekly newsletter with coverage on everything from product launches to software updates, this is your go-to source for the latest updates on all the best Apple content.

Let's say you want a brand new phone, but there aren't any significant discounts to be had. That's a common occurrence for Apple's iPhones, and the discounts you do get often come from carriers that insist you sign up for an expensive monthly data plan. That is why it's important to check the cost of the associated plans before you buy.

Not all deals rely on expensive plans either. You could find yourself paying close to full price for a new phone, but in the process get access to a cheaper data plan. It's all about doing the math and working out what data and perks you actually need, and whether it makes financial sense to lock into a specific plan for however many years are necessary.

It's well known that trading in your old devices is a great way to save money on a new phone. But not all trade-in offers are created equally, and it literally pays to check the small print and see what the details of the deal actually are.

Typically trade-ins operate on a system of new phones being worth the most, and the better the condition, the more you get back. But there are instances where those rules don't apply. For example, T-Mobile currently has a deal that offers up to $1,200 off the cost of an iPhone 18 Pro Max with an any condition trade in.

This means it doesn't matter how battered your phone may be, if you have one of the eligible devices you will get the full $1,200 credited to your account each month. Though, the newer devices still earn you more credit compared to older ones.

So you find a deal, and you're wondering whether it's actually a good one. Prices fluctuate all the time, and just because a discount is on offer doesn't necessarily mean a better one isn't around the corner. But how can you tell? You can't predict the future, but you can look back at the price history and see how the current discount compares to what's been offered before.

If you can see that a specific phone was $100 less than the current deal price within the last few months (such as during Prime Day sales), then there's a good chance that the price might drop a little more as we get closer to Black Friday itself. Though, I will admit that the multitude of mid-year price hikes does complicate things — because the price you paid in July won't be the same as the price you pay between now and the end of the year.

As for which tools to use, we're big fans of CamelCamelCamel, which lets you check the price history of unlocked phones on Amazon — with a quick comparison against third party retailers. That gives you an idea of how much a particular phone could cost, when not purchased from a carrier. As for carrier-sold devices, things are a little more complicated, though the deals tend to be focused on trade-ins and data plans rather than the cost of the device itself.

Just because you see a deal on a phone you like doesn't mean you should buy it right away. If you think the price could drop even further, then you obviously want to wait it out and see what happens. You'll be kicking yourself if you buy a new phone, and two days after it arrives you see it drop even further.

But, at the same time, these discounts are always fleeting and temporary. Put off checking out for too long and you could be faced with the prospect of paying full price again. So if you see a deal that you are happy with, there's no harm in confirming your purchase.

Brand new phones are always the most expensive, but just because they're available and discounted doesn't mean you have to buy one. As we've seen with Walmart's ongoing Black Friday sale, there are also plenty of discounts on older devices and refurbished models that are looking for a second chance at life. These phones are older, but they're also a lot cheaper than the latest model.

These deals are, admittedly, not as plentiful because those phones are officially out of production — so there aren't as many devices to go around. Still, the thing you need to remember about modern smartphones is that the differences aren't that major year-on-year. So a Galaxy S25 isn't that much of a step down from the Galaxy S26, and thanks to Samsung's commitment to 7 years of software support, a year-old phone isn't going to be a security risk for some time.

Black Friday sales officially begin Friday, November 27, 2026, and run throughout “Cyber Week,” the five-day period that runs from Thanksgiving through Cyber Monday, November 30, 2026. But Black Friday and Cyber Monday dates have expanded as retailers compete for customers. If you already have a cordless tool set and you want to expand your kit, or if you have a DIYer in your life who already has a particular brand of battery and you want to get them something else they can use, a single tool deal might make more sense.

#3416. The Punisher Officially Returns to Take on a Sci-Fi Villain in New Release

There aren't many people in the Marvel universe who would willingly pick a fight with Frank Castle, and those who do generally don't get the opportunity to regret it for very long. The ruthless vigilante, most recently portrayed by Jon Bernthal in the MCU, has spent decades making life miserable for criminals, often using methods that would make even Wolverine uncomfortable. But while the Punisher is perfectly capable of handling New York's worst villains, he's about to encounter something considerably more dangerous.

Marvel Comics has officially released Predator vs. Punisher #1, bringing Frank Castle face-to-face with the legendary alien hunter from Arnold Schwarzenegger's 1987 Sci-Fi action classic Predator. It's a limited run series, written by Frank Tieri, with artwork by Jesús Saíz and a main cover by Dustin Weaver.

The story transforms New York City into a hunting ground when a Predator arrives searching for worthy prey and sets its sights on Castle. Unfortunately, the alien's arrival also sparks chaos throughout the criminal underworld, with familiar Marvel villains including Kingpin, Jigsaw, Silvermane, and the Owl caught in the escalating violence.

Speaking with ComicBook, Tieri explained why bringing these two characters together was such an appealing prospect. "Well, for starters… are there any greater killing machines in comics than these two? That’s the fun of it here… Fans have debated for years which of these two pop culture icons of violence would come out on top if they were to ever go at it… and now they get to find out."

But it's worth noting that the Predator has just a couple of advantages that even Frank Castle might struggle with, and Tieri admitted that the Predator's physical superiority does make it an obvious favorite, but it's not like humans haven't killed Predators before.

"Well, if you look strictly at the tale of the tape, the Punisher would have no chance. The Predator is 7 feet tall, has superhuman strength, has better weaponry and is invisible half the time. And the Punisher at the end of the day is just a dude. A very deadly dude, but a dude nonetheless. But now here’s the thing… deadly dudes (And dudettes) have taken out Predators before. Dutch, Mike Harrigan, Naru, the cast of Killer of Killers, among others. So, does the Predator have the edge at the end of the day? $#*! yeah. But maybe don’t count Frank Castle out just yet…"

The first issue of Predator vs. Punisher was released November 11, 2026, and is available through comic book retailers and digital platforms. Stay tuned to Collider for all the latest news and updates on the biggest and best movies and shows heading to your favorite streaming platforms soon.

The HP OmniBook 5 14 impresses thanks to its lovely design, sharp OLED panel, strong performance, and astonishing battery life. Though it lacks HDR and has a so-so webcam, it’s a worthy alternative to the MacBook Neo for Windows users.

Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

The HP OmniBook 5 is the latest MacBook Neo rival on the market, and it makes a strong impression. Like Apple’s notebook, this budget laptop isn’t “cheap,” thanks to its striking color options and aluminum design. Along with its strong productivity performance and nearly 20-hour battery life, this also gives the equally wallet-friendly Dell XPS 13 reasons to sweat.

The compact, lightweight design is built for all-day travel, while the 14-inch display delivers strong colors and sharp 2K resolution. After class or work, you can unwind by watching your favorite videos.

Even though the display is more vivid than those on other budget Windows laptops, it doesn’t support HDR — which is odd for an OLED panel. Speaker quality is decent but rather thin, and the 1080p webcam can be a bit grainy even in well-lit rooms.

Despite some flaws, you’re getting your money’s worth with the HP OmniBook 5. Right now, it’s one of the best budget laptops and a worthy alternative to the MacBook Neo. Find out why in my full review!

1x HDMI, 2x USB-C, 1x 3.5mm headphone jack

1x HDMI, 2x USB-C, 1x 3.5mm headphone jack

Don't let the relatively low asking price fool you, as the HP OmniBook 5 is anything but cheap thanks to its eye-catching design, long-lasting battery life, and other excellent features.

Like the MacBook Neo and Dell XPS 13, the HP OmniBook 5 doesn’t look like a typical budget laptop. That's thanks to its thin, elegant all-aluminum design, which looks great and feels good to hold.

The lid flexes a bit when you press in on its center, but the laptop is otherwise very sturdy. At 12.3 x 8.62 x 0.46 inches and 2.5 pounds, this is a perfect laptop for all-day travel, since you’ll barely feel it in your backpack.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

I’m a big fan of the keyboard deck, thanks to its relatively spacious size and thick keycaps that make typing a breeze. The backlit keys are nicely spaced and have excellent travel distance. The touchpad isn’t as large as I’ve seen on other laptops, but it's plenty responsive and never fails to register your gestures.

You can technically open the laptop with one hand, though the lid is a bit too sturdy to make that easy. Even though it’s easier to open the laptop with two hands, I appreciate that the lid doesn’t wobble when you’re walking around with the laptop open.

Port selection is fairly generous for a laptop this thin. The left side has an HDMI port and two USB-C ports, while the right side has a single 3.5mm headphone jack. The USB-C ports are USB3, whereas the MacBook Neo has one USB3 port and a slower USB2 port. That means you can charge the OmniBook 5 via either USB-C port.

Lastly, the OmniBook 5 comes in one of four colors: Peony Pink, Smoke Silver, Soft Honeydew, and Starlit Blue. Our review unit’s Soft Honeydew (green) color is quite nice and certainly more striking than the silver or black laptops I typically review.

The 14-inch 1920 x 1200 OLED panel on the HP OmniBook is pretty solid for a laptop in this price range. It delivers decent brightness and oversaturated colors, which helps colors pop. You can see this in the image above, where a video clip of a rabbit basking in the sun appears bright, colorful, and sharp.

Our display benchmark results corroborate my eyes-on experience. The display’s brightness averages 272 nits, which is just shy of the marketed 300 nits. This is as bright as it gets, since the display doesn’t support HDR. Color reproduction numbers for the sRGB and DCI-P3 color gamuts are well above 100%, which accounts for the oversaturated hues.

As you can see above, the displays on the Dell XPS 13 (2026) and MacBook Neo can get much brighter with SDR content, not to mention HDR. Color reproduction is also closer to 100%, so colors look more natural. Color accuracy (Delta-E) is also slightly lower (0 is best) on the HP laptop compared to its rivals.

The touchscreen is as responsive as you’d expect from a Windows 11 machine. It always registered all my taps and swipes accurately. Since the hinge can drop flat, you could theoretically draw on this display more easily. However, since it lacks stylus support, you’d have to draw with your finger, which likely won’t be comfortable or as precise.

The HP OmniBook 5 has modest specs fitting its price. The $649 starting configuration has an Intel Core 5 315 “Wildcat Lake” chip, 8GB of RAM, 256GB of SSD storage, and lacks a touchscreen. Our $749 review unit is a step up, packing an Intel Core 5 320 CPU, 16GB of RAM, 512GB of storage, and a touch display.

This laptop is designed to handle the basics, such as web browsing, working in word processors, and streaming videos. I had no problem using HP’s notebook for my everyday work, which usually involves a dozen open Chrome tabs, light photo editing in GIMP, and the occasional YouTube video running in the background.

As you can see above, the HP OmniBook 5 fares well against similarly-priced budget laptops. In the Geekbench 6 CPU benchmark, its single- and multi-core scores are fairly close to the Dell XPS 13, which has the same Wildcat Lake processor and amount of memory. However, its SSD speeds (Blackmagic) and Handbrake (video transcoding) scores are noticeably lower.

Even though the MacBook Neo we reviewed has only 8GB of RAM, it still outperforms both of its Wildcat Lake-powered rivals by a large margin. The only area where Apple’s affordable MacBook lags is SSD speed. That says a lot about the rock-solid performance the Neo delivers.

Wildcat Lake is perfect for basic tasks, but it’s decidedly not built for graphically demanding gaming. In the 3DMark Wildlife Extreme test, which measures a machine’s graphical performance, the HP OmniBook 5 scored 2922 and averaged 18 frames per second.

That’s similar to the Dell XPS 13, though the MacBook Neo has an edge over both. Using its built-in benchmark tool, Borderlands 3 is unplayable at 10.5 fps at 1080p. The same is true for the Dell XPS 13 and MacBook Neo.

Even if the Dell XPS 13 and MacBook Neo have better displays and faster performance, HP’s OmniBook 5 smokes both in battery life.

In our battery life test, which involves continuous Wi-Fi web surfing with the display set to 150 nits of brightness, the OmniBook 5 ran for an astounding 19 hours and 52 minutes! As you can see below, its competitors don’t even come close. It's impressive that this humble laptop can last as long as a MacBook Pro.

There's a lot to like about the HP OmniBook 5, but its budget nature comes with some compromises.

If the HP OmniBook 5 were the only budget laptop like it, I’d likely overlook its lack of HDR support. However, given that the MacBook Neo and Dell XPS 13 do have HDR support, it’s something I can’t entirely ignore. That's why the display doesn’t get nearly as bright as those of its competitors.

In fairness to HP’s laptop, it does sport an OLED panel — something the MacBook Neo and Dell XPS 13 do not. As a result, this panel offers stronger contrast between dark and light elements than the Neo and XPS’ respective IPS panels. It also delivers bolder colors, which could be a plus for some folks.

The HP OmniBook 5 has a 1080p FHD IR camera. That’s certainly better than the 720p webcams that budget Windows laptops tend to pack. However, don’t expect the best picture or video quality here.

Even in my building’s well-lit lobby lounge, the picture I snapped is pretty grainy. Yes, you can still see me and the background clearly enough, but don’t expect to look your best.

The HP OmniBook 5 is yet another fantastic MacBook Neo rival for folks looking for a comparable budget Windows laptop. The sturdy design and long battery life are highlights, while the impressive OLED panel and strong everyday performance make for an all-around solid laptop that won’t break the bank.

The MacBook Neo still arguably has an edge thanks to its strong performance, brighter display, and seamless interoperability with Apple’s devices. But if you prefer Windows or want astounding battery life, the HP OmniBook 5 is a solid choice.

#3409. Update Your iPhone to Prevent People From Seeing iMessages They Shouldn't

Has this ever happened to you? You add someone new to an iMessage group chat, and wonder, "Huh, can they see any of the messages from before they were added?" The answer to that question is supposed to be "no." By design, new iMessage group chat members are only privy to texts that arrive after they were added. When they join, it's essentially a blank slate, as if you just created the group for the first time. At least, that's how it's intended to work.

As it turns out, there's a bug with iMessage that may allow new group chat members to see texts from before they were added to the chat. That's a problem, and not just for the iPhone users out there talking smack about people before inviting them to join the group chat. It means iMessage, and Apple's platforms in general, aren't working like they're supposed to be. You don't have to be talking behind people's backs to not want new members seeing existing chats. Maybe you're planning a surprise party for someone, and add them to the group once everyone's in on the plan; maybe the texts in the chat aren't relevant to the current group, and the person joining simply does not need to access them.

That's not all: There exists another security flaw that could allow remote hackers to join an iMessage group and receive new messages. You might add a new user to a group chat and inadvertently invite them to read all existing messages, while at the same time being attacked by a bad actor who can then intercept all future messages. Not good.

Luckily, there's currently a fix for these problems. Apple patched (and revealed) the bugs, along with seven other security flaws, with a series of software updates on Monday for iPhone, iPad, Mac, Apple Watch, and Vision Pro. Not all of the updates include patches for these two iMessage flaws—specifically, some of the updates for older Apple devices. But the rest, including iOS 27.2.1, macOS 27.2.1, macOS 26.7.3, macOS 15.8.3, watchOS 27.2.1, and visionOS 27.2.1, include the iMessage patches.

Each update includes its own list of patches, but, for this article, I'll take a look at the nine patches in iOS 27.2.1. You'll find the two iMessage bugs, plus seven other patches, in the list below:

AirPlay: Impact: An attacker in Bluetooth range may be able to bypass the rate limit on pairing code attempts. Description: A logic issue was addressed with improved state management. CVE-2026-113968: Apple

App Intents: Impact: An app may be able to access sensitive user data. Description: An authorization issue was addressed with improved state management. CVE-2026-113963: László Várady

Bluetooth: Impact: An attacker in Bluetooth range may be able to corrupt process memory. Description: A use-after-free issue was addressed with improved memory management. CVE-2026-113970: Apple

brotli: Impact: Processing maliciously crafted input may lead to memory corruption. Description: An out-of-bounds write issue was addressed with improved input validation. CVE-2026-111497

CoreUtils: Impact: A malicious Bluetooth device may be able to establish a pairing without user interaction. Description: This issue was addressed with improved checks. CVE-2026-113965: Apple

CoreUtils: Impact: An attacker in Bluetooth range may be able to bypass the rate limit on pairing code attempts and pair with a device without user interaction. Description: A logic issue was addressed with improved state management. CVE-2026-113964: an anonymous researcher

Messages: Impact: A remote attacker may be able to join an iMessage group chat and receive its messages. Description: An authorization issue was addressed with improved validation. CVE-2026-113961: an anonymous researcher

Messages: Impact: A user added to an iMessage group may be able to access messages sent before they joined. Description: This issue was addressed by removing the vulnerable code. CVE-2026-113960: an anonymous researcher

Rapportd: Impact: An attacker on the same network may be able to bypass the rate limit on AirPlay pairing code attempts. Description: A logic issue was addressed with improved state management. CVE-2026-113969: Apple

For a full accounting of the patches included in the other security updates, check out Apple's official security releases site.

To install Apple's latest security updates, you'll simply need to update your device as you usually do. On iPhone, iPad, Apple Watch, and Vision Pro, head to Settings > General > Software Update; on Mac, go to System Settings > General > Software Update. Here, follow the on-screen instructions to download and install the latest version of your device's software.

#3408. Today’s macOS updates fix security gap involving eMudhra certificates

Apple today released macOS updates that address a security gap involving compromised eMudhra certificates, after initially blocking them in Safari, Mail, and other apps in October. Here are the details.

A few weeks ago, Mozilla reported that private keys of eight intermediate certificate authorities operated by eMudhra, an Indian digital certification company, had been compromised.

In essence, these certificates are used to establish trust in digital certificates that verify website identities and enable secure connections.

With access to the compromised private keys, bad actors could potentially create fraudulent certificates that appear legitimate, allowing them to impersonate websites and intercept sensitive user information.

In response to the compromise, Apple began automatically blocking the affected certificates on October 19, followed by additional protections on October 23.

These changes were delivered through automatic certificate configuration updates, meaning users didn’t need to install a macOS update to be protected.

While these measures protected Safari, Mail, and apps that use Apple’s networking and security frameworks, they didn’t cover all of macOS, as certain command-line tools, including curl and git, could still accept the compromised certificates.

At the time, Apple published a support article with instructions for administrators to manually address this remaining security gap, while promising a fix in a future macOS update.

Today, Apple updated the document to confirm that the fix is now available.

As Apple explains, macOS 27.2.1, macOS 26.7.3, and macOS 15.8.3, released earlier today, prevent the affected command-line tools from accepting the compromised certificates, eliminating the need for administrators to manually address the issue.

The updates also remove five root CA certificates from /etc/ssl/cert.pem, including three additional eMudhra certificates that weren’t part of Apple’s original manual workaround.

Still, for users who are unable to install the latest macOS updates, Apple continues to provide instructions for manually addressing the issue in its support document, along with the names and SHA-256 fingerprints of the 12 affected certificates and five root CA certificates removed by the updates.

Apple also notes that “some apps and tools include their own list of root CA certificates and don’t use Apple’s block or /etc/ssl/cert.pem,” and advises users to contact the developer of those apps and tools.

To read Apple’s full support document, follow this link.

As we first reported ... Bunnie and Jelly are going through a high-profile split -- though they've kept it mostly amicable in the public eye.

#3406. 10 Classic Rock Songs That Belong in These TV Shows

There's something magical that happens when the theme song for a TV series fits perfectly. The Rembrandt's "I'll Be There For You" is intrinsically linked to Friends, with its upbeat ode to close friendships. The theme to The Brady Bunch sums up the premise of the show in a catchy, never-leave-your-head tune. Nerf Herder's theme for Buffy the Vampire Slayer marries modern rock with gothic horror, an ideal match for a show that does much the same.

But there's a whole wealth of classic rock songs that would do the same thing, yet they remain unused. The CSI franchise famously used songs from The Who, the 1987-1990 military drama Tour of Duty used the Rolling Stones classic "Paint It, Black," and that's pretty much where it ends. It's a shame, and to prove it, here are 10 classic rock songs that simply belong in certain TV shows, where they are a much better fit than what they have already.

The 2017-2022 legal drama The Good Fight saw Diane Lockhart (Christine Baranski) and her goddaughter Maia (Rose Leslie) forced out of their legal firm one year after the events of The Good Wife, due to a financial scam that ruins the reputation of the latter while draining the savings of the former. They are starting again from scratch, joining a law firm that has made a name for itself by tackling police brutality cases. As the series progresses, storylines see them taking on such issues as the MeToo movement, online harassment, and the alt-right. They are, legitimately, "fighting the good fight," and there is no better way to stress that from the start than with Triumph's 1981 hit "Fight the Good Fight," a song about resilience and persistence in the face of life's difficulties. Thematically and nominally, it works.

Prison Break is about a man trying to escape prison. AC/DC's "Jailbreak" is about a man trying to escape prison. How no one saw to bring the two together is just shy of incomprehensible. In fairness, Prison Break's Lincoln Burrows (Dominic Purcell) is on death row for a crime he didn't commit, while Bon Scott's friend most certainly did commit a crime, murdering a man who was messing with his bae. And while both did escape, Lincoln did so successfully, with the show becoming less Prison Break-y and more big government conspiracy, while Bon's poor friend got a bullet in the back, just as he thought he was free. Just stick with the stuff in between, and you're gold.

Full confession: the opening theme song to Baywatch, "I'm Always Here" by Jimi Jamison, is already a pretty good 90s rocker, with lyrics ("I'll be ready... I won't let you out of my sight") that fit perfectly with the premise of ever-vigilant lifeguards on Malibu Beach. But the ending theme, "Current of Love" by David Hasselhoff? Um, no. So, for the upcoming reboot, we here at Collider have a suggestion. Keep "I'm Always Here" — you don't mess with what works — and ditch the Hoff mess. In its place, use the Beach Boys classic "California Girls." Not their version, mind you, but David Lee Roth's 1984 cover. Let's face it: we all know why Baywatch was so popular, and it wasn't for its riveting storylines. So surrender to the fact that at least half of the audience is in it for women — California girls — in red bikinis, running in slow motion across the beach, and own it by using Roth's cover over the end credits, with its lascivious edge more in tune than the Beach Boys' rather innocent original.

I Love Lucy stands as one of television's greatest, most iconic sitcoms, coming in at No. 2 on Collider's list of the 10 Best Shows in Network TV History. It centered around Lucy Ricardo (Lucille Ball), a middle-class homemaker in New York, and her husband Ricky (Desi Arnaz), the head bandleader at the Tropicana nightclub. The series took full advantage of Ball's uncanny comedic talent, with the plans she makes to be a part of show business always falling apart in spectacular fashion. She drove Ricky crazy, but he loved her all the same. If only there was a song that spoke to such a situation (that isn't "Weird Al" Yankovic's "Ricky"). Oh wait, there is: 1988's "She Drives Me Crazy" by Fine Young Cannibals. Of course, the 31 years between the premiere of I Love Lucy and the release of the song would have made such a connection difficult. But the song's description of a man trapped in a dichotomous dilemma of being driven nuts by his partner, yet unable to walk away because his love for her is all-consuming, is tailor-made for the series.

How does a 2006 speed/power metal anthem fit in with the renowned fantasy drama Game of Thrones? Far, far better than you might expect. The epic feel of the seven-minute-long "Through the Fire and the Flames" by DragonForce matches the epic scope of the series, for one. Both hinge on themes of war and survival, with the song telling the tale of warriors riding out on a cold winter's morning, facing death and enduring pain as they fight through the land, closely mirroring the trials that befall those in Westeros. At a rapid-fire 200 BPM, the song stirs up adrenaline just as the show's big battle sequences do. And last but not least, there's a literal fit as well, with the House Targaryen words of "Fire and Blood," and Daenerys Targaryen (Emilia Clarke) rising from the actual fire and flame of the funeral pyre, an easy connection with the title of DragonForce's biggest hit.

A speed metal song for a show like Game of Thrones still might be a push, but for a show like 24, where urgency is a key part of the premise, it works like a hot damn, and Anthrax has just the one: "Got the Time." The cover of Joe Jackson's 1979 song is on Anthrax's 1990 album Persistence of Time, a title that suits the premise of the series accurately. That premise sees counter-terrorist federal agent Jack Bauer (Kiefer Sutherland) race against a real-time clock, 24 hours, to stop terrorist plots. 9, in fact, one for each season. The idea that time is working against you, trapping you in a mad, desperate rush, is a motif shared by both "Got the Time" and 24, and that thrash metal pacing is a reflection of the adrenalin-soaked, chaotic pace of Bauer's unenviable task.

Sure, it's already been used as the CSI: Crime Scene Investigation theme song, and there isn't really a strong argument that can be made for its inclusion, but we maintain that "Who Are You" by The Who should be in the long-running sci-fi series Doctor Who. There's just something absolutely delicious about the three-peat of the word "who" that generates the feeling of a missed opportunity. Plus, it would open the door for an Abbott and Costello-like moment:

Now if only there was a way to bring in Cindy-Lou Who and the Whos down in Who-ville...

Like "Jailbreak"/Prison Break above, using the Talking Head's 1977 track for the 2006-2013 (and on) Showtime series Dexter seems like a no-brainer, yet it didn't happen. The series centers on Dexter Morgan (Michael C. Hall), a forensic technician for the Miami Metro Police Department by day, a vigilante serial killer by night, while the song's lyrics reflect the thoughts of a killer's mind... and it isn't unreasonable to associate the killer of Psycho Killer with Dexter Morgan. The steady rhythm is like Dexter's ritualistic daily habits, unchanging, while the layering of its, no pun intended, killer bassline and flashes of frenetic guitar give an emotional depiction of Dexter's inner conflict. The lyrics, meanwhile, coupled with David Byrne's staccato delivery of them, give voice to the killer's inner monologue, much like Dexter's "Dark Passenger," and to the disconnection from human emotion. Sigh... they should have at least taken a stab at it. Apologies for the sharp wit.

Michael Scott (Steve Carell) may have loved being at work, but the rest of the staff at the Scranton branch of Dunder Mifflin simply want to get through their workweek, escape unscathed from Michael's inanity, and start the weekend. That's why Loverboy's "Working for the Weekend" makes a perfect match for The Office. The series works as a brilliant satire of the 9-to-5 office job, targeting everyday routines, pointless bureaucracy (the assistant to the regional manager role being one), incompetent management, and coping with its soul-crushing monotony. A song like "Working for the Weekend" not only speaks to the average employee's mindset, but its high-energy would be a funny, ironic contrast to that mundane office work environment The Office so cleverly skewers.

We could get into how the eerie whistling and haunting saxophone of "Spooky" by Classics IV matches the dark, gothic atmosphere of Netflix's Wednesday. We could discuss how the vibe of the retro soul/soft rock tune, with its traces of psychedelia, fits in nicely with the music that already populates the series. But ultimately, the reason why "Spooky" belongs in Wednesday comes down to one single line:

"Love is kinda crazy with a spooky little girl like you."

And no one's spookier than Jenna Ortega's Wednesday Addams.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

#3405. This AirPods Feature Fixed My Biggest Problem With Listening to Podcasts to Fall Asleep

We're highlighting the small changes—from useful new gadgets, to fresh productivity techniques, to efficient hacks—that are improving our lives on a weekly basis.

There's lots to recommend about podcasts (and lots of podcasts to recommend), but one of their biggest benefits—for me, anyway—has little to do with what a particular show is about or even who hosts it: They're great for dissociating. I often have a podcast playing to distract my anxious brain from whatever I'm worried about (which, in 2026, is usually slightly less than everything).

Any time I don't want to be alone with my thoughts (say, when commuting or doing mindless chores), I can put on a podcast and be entertained by a couple of goobers talking about movies rather than spinning my wheels about my son's middle school applications. And there's no time I want to disassociate from reality more than bedtime.

For years I've used podcasts as a non-pharmaceutical sleep aid, and few things are more effective at helping me drop off quickly. Unfortunately, for years this also meant that once I fell asleep, the podcast kept playing. I have my podcast app set to delete episodes once finished, so if it was a show I cared about, I'd need to do a lot of redownloading and scrubbing through to find where I left off—that is, until I upgraded my earbuds to the AirPods Pro 3.

The AirPods Pro 3 launched alongside iOS 26 in the fall of 2025 with flashy features like vastly improved noise cancellation, Live Translation, Heart Rate Sensing, and hearing health settings, all of them quite welcome on a set of $250 premium earbuds. But the best new AirPods feature was one I didn't even know about when I decided to upgrade my four-year-old Beats Fit Pro.

In the AirPods settings (accessible via your iPhone's Settings app), if you tap Audio & Routing and scroll down, you'll see an option to turn on a setting called Pause Media When Falling Asleep. I don't think I need to tell you what this setting does. I can tell you that it works great.

According to Apple, the feature works by sensing when you're drifting off using the earbuds' built-in accelerometer to track your movement (or lack thereof). Once your earbuds have determined that you're falling asleep, they will pause your audio for you. And it isn't just the 2025 AirPods Pro 3 that support it—it also works on the second-generation AirPods Pro as well as the AirPods 4 and the AirPods 5.

I'll admit that I don't really understand how the AirPods Pro 3 can tell I'm falling asleep versus just lying very still, but I've never had them pause accidentally during active listening. Conversely, whenever I go back to the podcast I was listening to the night before, I'll find that the audio paused within a minute or two of the last part I remember hearing.

The AirPods Pro 3 aren't the only earbuds with a feature like this, but you'll most often only find it in dedicated "sleep earbuds" designed specifically for the purpose. While many of those offer extra health features like the ability to track your sleep cycles, I'm not really interested in that (my Apple Watch does most of it, and I don't look at that data anyway). Pausing my audio when I'm asleep is really all I need, and the AirPods Pro 3 do it well enough that I don't need to bother with a pair of dedicated bedtime buds.

#3404. Apple Intelligence completes regulatory registration for iPad and Mac in China

Apple has completed an important regulatory step ahead of Apple Intelligence’s expected launch in China this December. Here are the details.

In late October, Apple published a press release on its Chinese Newsroom website confirming its intention to launch Apple Intelligence in China this December, as part of iOS 27.3.

Apple went on to release the first iOS 27.3 developer beta a few days later, allowing users in China to test Apple Intelligence ahead of its public launch.

In its press release, however, Apple also noted that the initial rollout would be limited to iPhones, as support for other platforms was still pending regulatory approval.

Now, as spotted by Reuters, Apple Intelligence “has been ‌registered for use on tablets and laptops in China, Shanghai’s cyberspace regulator said on Monday.”

For context, generative AI services must complete a regulatory registration process before they can launch publicly in China.

Apple Intelligence, which, in China, relies on Alibaba’s Qwen model to power certain AI features, had already received regulatory approval for iPhones in July, following months of delays and negotiations with Chinese authorities.

With today’s registration, Apple has cleared another regulatory hurdle ahead of Apple Intelligence’s launch in China. However, the company has yet to confirm whether iPad and Mac support will also arrive in December.

#3398. Canadian court certifies class action against Apple over Google search deal

A British Columbia Supreme Court judge has certified a class action against Apple over allegations that its search agreement with Google stifled competition and inflated advertising prices. Here are the details.

In recent years, Apple’s deal with Alphabet to make Google the default search engine on Safari has drawn regulatory attention in the US, the UK, and Australia, while related search competition concerns have also come under scrutiny in the EU and Japan.

While the details of each investigation differ, they all raise concerns about the impact of Google’s dominance in search, as well as the extent to which its agreements with other companies might be limiting competition.

More recently, Apple’s agreement with Google received significant attention during the US Department of Justice’s antitrust case against the search giant, which included testimony from Apple executives Eddy Cue and John Giannandrea. The latter joined Apple from Google in 2018 and led its AI efforts until stepping down earlier this year.

As a result of the US case, a federal judge ruled in August 2024 that Google had illegally maintained its monopoly in online search through anticompetitive agreements, including its deal with Apple.

Now, evidence presented during that trial has become central to a class action against Apple in Canada, which a British Columbia Supreme Court judge recently certified.

The case was initially brought in 2021 by Spark Event Rentals Ltd., an event rental company based in British Columbia. The plaintiff alleged that Apple and Google conspired to limit competition in the search market, allowing Google to charge advertisers artificially inflated prices.

Apple, meanwhile, argued that its agreement with Google was a legitimate distribution arrangement rather than an unlawful conspiracy. The company also maintained that Google was the appropriate defendant, describing itself as an “innocent bystander.”

Interestingly, the lawsuit originally named both Apple and Google as defendants, but the plaintiff later dropped Google from the case following a dispute over an arbitration clause in its advertising contracts.

With Apple now the sole defendant, Justice Thomas has allowed the case to proceed as a class action, finding sufficient grounds to examine whether Google’s payments discouraged Apple from developing its own search engine.

The lawsuit seeks financial compensation for advertisers who allegedly overpaid for Google search ads, and the court has also allowed the question of punitive damages to proceed.

The class action covers Canadian residents who purchased search ads from Google since 2005, when Apple and Google first agreed to make Google the default search engine on Safari in exchange for a share of advertising revenue.

Importantly, the ruling does not establish that Apple engaged in anticompetitive conduct, but simply allows the allegations to proceed as a class action.

The central proposition raised by these pleadings is that Apple could have used its resources and distribution network to enter the search engine market, but chose not to because Google paid Apple billions of dollars in revenue-share payments to make Google the default search provider on Apple products. This arrangement gave Google market power, enabling it to charge supracompetitive advertising prices on search engines.

In my view, this pleads a common purpose to perform an act prohibited by s 45 of the Competition Act, such that it is not “clear and obvious” that the plaintiff has not pleaded an agreement between Google and Apple not to compete in the search engine market.

At one point in his decision, Justice Thomas cites Giannandrea’s testimony and directly quotes Cue’s from the US antitrust trial, before concluding that “this provides some basis in fact, supporting the inference that Apple did not compete with Google in the search engine market because of its Agreement with Google.”

Interestingly, the judge also acknowledges Apple’s objections to the evidence, agreeing that “the plaintiff has cherry-picked evidence to support his case,” but adding that, in his view, “it is appropriate to do so at this stage in the proceedings.”

With the class action greenlit, the case can now move forward toward trial, though no date has been announced yet.

#3395. 10 Hacks Every Waze User Should Know

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

Waze is a crowdsourced navigation app designed to help you get where you're going as quickly and with as much information about your route as possible. Where Google Maps and Apple Maps offer relatively straightforward directions, Waze tries to outsmart these alternatives by integrating real-time community feedback about hazards, speed traps, road closures, and more. If you are switching to Waze or using it alongside your other navigation tools, these are the hacks to help you maximize everything the app has to offer.

If you find yourself losing track of time or running late for events, Waze can notify you when it's time to leave—based on your current location and live traffic—so you arrive on schedule. You can set up "Time to leave" reminders in advance for individual planned drives, or you can sync your calendar to receive notifications for scheduled events. Calendar sync connects to your device's default calendar app, but you can change this to a third-party alternative if you prefer. Calendar events must include a navigable address to trigger reminders, and you must select Plan a drive in Waze for the event.

Waze has a feature called "child reminders," which are notifications to check for children before you get out of the car. This is clearly an incredibly important use case, but you can also use these alerts for custom messages, like "Don't forget the groceries!" In Waze, tap the menu button > Settings > Reminders > Child reminder and select Custom message.

Variable speed limits, especially on unfamiliar routes, can result in you speeding when you don't mean to. But Waze can alert you if you exceed a customized speed threshold so you aren't caught by surprise or at higher risk of being ticketed. From the menu, go to Settings > Speedometer and turn on Show speedometer. Tap Speeding threshold to select what limit you want to trigger alerts, and turn on Alert at threshold if you want Waze to play a sound.

Waze offers a wealth of information on routes to help drivers navigate obstacles and hazards, but this can clutter your map and distract you from the most critical information, especially in congested, high-traffic areas. Waze says it limits and prioritizes alerts automatically, but you can actually customize which alerts you see based on what's most important to you. From the menu, go to Settings > Alerts and reports > Reports and select the relevant alerts.

In the same Alerts and reports menu, you can enable Alert while driving, which will give you an audio warning and an onscreen pop-up about your selected hazards. This allows you to run navigation via a different map app (like Google Maps or Apple Maps) in the foreground while still getting Waze data in the background.

Waze integrates with toll road and HOV lane passes, so if you have an express or fast lane subscription, your route will optimize for it. If you don't, Waze can still account for HOV lane eligibility if you tell it how many passengers are in your car. From the menu, go to Settings > Toll and HOV passes and tap the plus icon to add your pass(es) from the list. If you need to add your passenger count instead, you can do so from View routes and enable the HOV option.

If you're driving through an unfamiliar, highly congested, or poorly designed area, you can ask Waze to help you avoid tricky maneuvers, such as crossing multiple lanes of traffic or turning left at intersections without lights. This prioritizes ease over speed using protected green arrows, roundabouts, and right turns. From the menu, go to Settings > Navigation, Avoid difficult intersections and select Always. You can also ask Waze to avoid toll roads, ferries, freeways, and unpaved roads.

Waze has a built-in audio player that syncs with your preferred listening platform—such as Spotify, YouTube Music, and Pandora—so you can control your music without having to navigate between apps. (As Waze is a Google product, Apple Music isn't included.) Simply tap the music icon on the map to select your audio player and hit Accept. If you don't see the icon, go to Settings > Audio player and turn on Show on the map.

If you want to make audio directions more interesting, you can select a celebrity or character voice to help you navigate. Recent appearances include Bill Hader's Cat in the Hat and Ziggy Marley. Tap the speaker icon > Current voice to search for the voice or language you want to use. You can also record directions in your own voice.

I love my peace lily. Its glossy green leaves and elegant white blooms add a gorgeous touch to my home — except lately, it’s been all leaves and no flowers.

To figure out where I’m going wrong, I asked the experts how to get it blooming again. Thankfully, it doesn’t necessarily mean it’s unhealthy; often a few adjustments to its growing conditions, along with some patience, can make a difference.

Having a peace lily that doesn’t flower is a common frustration for owners, according to Elizabeth Waddington, garden designer and writer at First Tunnels. But she says, “Often slight adjustments to the light levels, warmth, water provided, or other growing conditions can encourage blooms to form.”

And, of course, another reason why your peace lily might not be flowering yet is that it’s simply immature and not at the flowering stage. Plus, they don’t flower year-round.

Most commonly, houseplant peace lilies will flower in spring and summer. “Don’t panic if you’re not seeing any growth during the winter months, as this is when they slow down,” says David Denyer, florist and gardening expert at Eflorist.

However, this may change if you see them growing in their natural, tropical environment, with Waddington adding, “If well cared for indoors, in optimal growing conditions, peace lilies can flower at any time, and may even flower more than once a year.”

Unfortunately, peace lilies don’t flower indefinitely. Denyer says, “A peace lily flower will usually last for a month, or even two with the proper care, before changing to black or brown.” Did you know it’s not really a flower?The white section of a peace lily, often called a flower, is actually a modified leaf called a spathe or bract.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

The best way to keep your peace lily flowering for longer is to make sure it is cared for properly. “If your peace lily is struggling to bloom at all, this usually means it’s needing a bit more care and attention,” says Denyer.

“Flowering takes a lot of energy, so it’s key that during the growing season you feed your plant little and often,” explains Denyer. And he suggests using a balanced, water-soluble fertilizer every few weeks from April to October. During winter, he recommends reducing the feed to every 4-6 weeks, to maintain your peace lily without encouraging excessive growth or overwhelming your plant.

As a tropical plant, peace lilies prefer a consistently warm temperature, and they can be particularly sensitive to temperature changes; that’s why Denyer says it’s important that you adjust your care for them as the seasons change.

“One of the biggest mistakes people can make when caring for their peace lily is positioning it near windows and air vents,” Denyer explains. “Although you may think your peace lily will love the light that comes from being right next to the window, exposing it to cold drafts is actually detrimental to the health of your plant.”He adds that if exposed to low temperatures for a long time, you may notice your peace lily wilts, and it can even die. Similarly, placing your peace lily near a heat source can damage it, too.

The ideal temperaturePeace lilies don’t adjust well to unstable temperatures and perform best between 64 and 80°F (18 to 27°C), according to Waddington.

While peace lilies need light, which can be lacking in winter, Denyer says not to be tempted to move your plant into direct sunlight, as this will scorch the leaves. Instead, move it to a position where it can gain bright, indirect light or use a suitable grow light above it. This Aokrean Grow Light for Indoor Plants is just $17 at Amazon.Placing your plant next to a window may also expose it to cold drafts, which it will hate.

“As tropical plants, peace lilies enjoy relatively humid conditions,” says Waddington. If the air in your home is dry, especially during winter, she suggests grouping houseplants together, using a room humidifier, or placing the plant on a pebble tray with water, ensuring the bottom of the pot stays above the waterline.

She also suggests misting the leaves, but warns, “Make sure you do this in the morning so that the excess water can evaporate, or you may experience some fungal growth on your peace lily.”

What’s more, because peace lilies love humidity, they are the perfect houseplant for a steamy bathroom!

These gardening gloves provide an excellent grip and have a comfortable fit around the wrist, plus they are breathable and machine washable and available in three sizes. They are perfect when you need a medium-duty glove that provides dexterity. Plus, they come in a pack of two.

You should continue watering your peace lily regularly throughout winter, but Denyer says you may need to adjust your watering schedule. “Your weekly watering routine may turn into every 10 days during the winter months,” he says.

He also adds that peace lilies like consistently moist soil, so when the top inch of soil is dry, you can give it a little bit of water to maintain the plant’s health. But be careful not to overwater your plant, which can lead to waterlogged soil, or leave it completely dry, which can cause the leaves to turn brown.

#3389. Ring's New $250 Indoor Camera Drone Sounds Terrifying

Ring made its name with its smart doorbells with built-in cameras, and now sells more indoor cameras than any other company, capturing more than 40% of the market. When you've already moved tens of millions of devices (enough to raise serious concerns about their use as part of the surveillance state), you always need to keep innovating, and today, the company announced a product it has been working on for a decade: an indoor camera drone powered by artificial intelligence. I got a chance to check it out during a media event yesterday, and I can report that, as harbingers of our dystopian future go, it is only mildly terrifying.

The drone camera is one of two products in the company's new Ring Robotics line, alongside a "rover cam" that looks kind of like the canister of a vacuum cleaner attached to an iPad. While the Ring Rover Cam is priced at $999.99 and targeted at businesses, the Ring Drone Cam is a much more affordable $249.99, reasonable enough that it will appeal to consumers looking for another way to keep (robot) eyes on their stuff.

The drone camera records 2K video and has a 148-degree field of view and the ability to rotate 360 degrees. It works with existing Ring cameras, doorbells, sensors, and alarms, as well as the Alexa Home Map. It has a flight time of eight minutes, and once it returns to its base station, it takes around an hour to fully recharge (eight minutes on the dock will give it one minute in the air).

As Ring founder Jamie Siminoff explained during the preview event, the company has been trying to build a workable camera drone for around a decade, but couldn't overcome certain design challenges until the advancement of AI models that allow the device to handle most of the computing—from route programming to threat detection—via the cloud, so the drones can be smaller and lighter.

According to Ring, when setting up the Ring Drone Cam, you carry it around your house, allowing it to map the interior. It will "intelligently identify rooms and suggest patrol points: spots worth extra attention." When sent out on "patrol," the drone's AI pilot will travel between hotspots, sensing and avoiding furniture and other obstacles along the way.The Ring Drone Cam works with other Ring cameras, so if an alert is triggered somewhere in your home—say, a window opening unexpectedly—the drone will take off to investigate. It has a built-in security light that will make its presence known, so it can also act as a deterrent, though the screaming sound of its spinning propellers will accomplish that just as well.

According to Ring, the drone camera can deliver peace of mind whether you're home or away, and admittedly I do like the idea of being able to check on my pets or make sure no pipes have burst while I'm at work or on vacation (though admittedly you can get the same sort of monitoring without involving an AI device that looks like a mini version of the flying robots from The Terminator).

I admit that the Ring Drone Cam seems pretty cool, provided I don't think about it too much. I don't know that I really feel the need to have every inch of my home covered in security cameras, but I do like the idea that the drone could, for example, go to check out what's going on if one of my smoke alarms' temperature sensors reports that one spot in the house is all of a sudden hotter than it should be.

If you're ready to enter this brave new world of security, you'll have to wait a bit longer: The Ring Drone Camera isn't expected to ship until January 2027, but you can sign up to be alerted when it is available for preorder now.

#3388. Google DeepMind analysis proves Signal and WhatsApp encryption is secure

The Signal protocol has long been considered the gold standard for end-to-end encrypted messaging, with Edward Snowden a notable advocate. Now a Google DeepMind analysis has “formally verified” the security of the protocol.

In addition to its use in the Signal app, the same protocol is also used by WhatsApp and Google Messages, and the work has been described as “a landmark development” …

“Formal verification” is the term given to mathematically proving or disproving that a cryptographic algorithm or protocol satisfies its security claims under all conditions. It guarantees that there is no situation in which the protocol will fail. This is a far higher standard than traditional testing methods which seek to find vulnerabilities but cannot promise that others do not exist.

Using agentic AI to carry out formal verification is a huge breakthrough for cryptography and AI alike. It is, however, extremely computationally demanding, so Google told Wired it’s unclear as yet how practical it will be to use it more broadly.

DeepMind researchers emphasize that their findings are just one milestone in a larger process. “We are very excited by this result, but there is a long distance to go before we are able to scale this to all the software of the world, and we want to do that,” Swarat Chaudhuri, a DeepMind research scientist, tells WIRED.

It’s important to note that the validation is for the protocol itself rather than the Signal app as a whole. However, encouragement can be taken from the fact that when tested against older versions of Signal that contained known vulnerabilities, it identified those and flagged them as failing formal verification.

Also worth stating is that Google was able to build on some past formal verification work already completed without the use of AI. This analysis took four weeks, and the scale of resources required has not yet been disclosed, so we shouldn’t expect a whole array of other protocols to be validated overnight. All the same, this is a very big deal.

There have been so many heist thrillers in movies and TV that it’s tough to find a fresh angle on the well-worn subgenre. The new Apple TV series “12 12 12” attempts to make its heist story stand out by dividing it among three timelines, inspired by a dubious-sounding FBI statistic quoted at the beginning of each episode: A high-level, professional heist requires 12 months of planning, 12 hours to execute, and if the robbers aren’t caught within 12 days, they never will be.

That gives creators Jim Keeble and Dudi Appleton a strict format to follow, but fracturing the narrative mostly serves as a distraction from the basic heist-thriller elements.

Just because it’s basic doesn’t mean that it’s bad, and as a connoisseur of this type of story, I still mostly had fun with “12 12 12.” Eight episodes is a long time to spend on a single crime, though, and the momentum flags as the season progresses, especially when the creators are simply filling in the gaps for events that viewers have already seen.

Jamie Dornan and Anthony Mackie are compelling as the central criminal and cop, respectively, and “12 12 12” is slick and propulsive enough to make for a mildly entertaining watch, even if it’s far from reinventing the heist thriller.

Although it could be confusing to follow three separate timelines of the same characters engaged in the same project, “12 12 12” makes it relatively simple, with onscreen graphics indicating exactly which part of which segment is taking place at any given time. The individual tracks (months, hours, days) unfold in a linear fashion, so that the first episode begins with the first month of planning, the first hour of the robbery, and the first day of the getaway. Each episode moves the story forward in all three time periods.

In that way, “12 12 12” is rarely disorienting, but the structure also robs the story of some potential suspense. Viewers already know that the planning stage will lead to an actual heist, and that the heist will succeed well enough for the perpetrators to get away. Even so, Keeble and Appleton are able to consistently deploy surprise twists, and they use the show’s structure for misdirection, when something that happens in one particular time period turns out not to be what it seems once information from later or earlier is revealed.

Laid out in a straightforward manner, the plot is pretty standard. Reformed robber Paul Galvin (Dornan) is drawn back into criminal activity by his screw-up older brother Bobby (Jack Kesy), who’s gotten himself in trouble with a powerful French mobster. That menacing crime boss threatens to kill Paul’s wife Severine (Agathe Rousselle) and his unborn child if he doesn’t take on the job of stealing nearly $1 billion in cash stored by the Russian mafia in a Swiss bank.

Sign up to the weekly Tom's Streaming Guide to stay in the loop with the latest releases and top recommendations across your favorite streaming services. We’ve got you covered with a complete guide on what’s worth watching.

Meanwhile, FBI agent Jack Strickland (Mackie) has transferred to Europe so that he can track the Galvins after a failed takedown in Newark that left Jack’s partner dead.

To pull off the heist, Paul recruits an extensive crew that includes his drilling-expert father-in-law, the bank’s disgraced head of security, and a contortionist who can fit inside a safety deposit box, among others. Most of the characters get limited screen time, and even a recognizable star like Kali Reis of “True Detective” is little more than a cog in the heist plan, playing an expert in train engineering who plans the getaway. It’s a bit disappointing given the lengthy running time that there isn’t more room for character development beyond the combative relationship between the Galvin brothers.

That fraternal dynamic wears out quickly, but Jack has a more complex, rewarding arc, as he has to transcend his desire for revenge against the Galvins and find a way to move forward. The most compelling relationship in “12 12 12” is between Jack and Swiss police detective Lena (Sallie Harmsen), who goes from wary colleague to devoted ally to something more. Their scenes together have more emotional resonance than all of the Galvin brothers’ macho bluster.

Even if the characters never acquire that much depth, the plot moves so briskly that there’s rarely a chance to stop and wonder what makes these people tick. There are a couple of exciting car chases, especially one through the streets of Zurich in the first episode, plus plenty of nail-biting moments as the crew tries to solve various problems under the threat of imminent discovery or danger.

If nothing else, “12 12 12” puts its budget to great use, with action that spans multiple European countries and set pieces that include a giant avalanche and a narrowly avoided train collision. It’s not as lively or witty as the “Ocean’s” movies, and the rivalry between Paul and Jack has nothing on Robert De Niro and Al Pacino in “Heat.” But it holds the audience’s attention almost all the way to the end, until a final episode that has one or two superfluous conclusions.

The timeline trickery proves to be largely superfluous, too, but it keeps viewers on their toes and offers a few satisfying “aha” moments. That’s about all a heist thriller needs. If the formula works, there’s no reason to mess with it.

Josh Bell is a freelance writer and movie/TV critic based in Las Vegas. He's the former film editor of Las Vegas Weekly and has written about movies and TV for Vulture, Inverse, CBR, Crooked Marquee and more. With comedian Jason Harris, he co-hosts the podcast Awesome Movie Year.
