#3286. Build a Hidden Lock With a Magnetic Imager

Stephen Cass is the special projects editor at IEEE Spectrum.

Only a programmable secret gesture with a magnet can open this lockbox. (Or a hammer. It’s a proof of concept.)

Like many a nerd, I have a certain fascination with locks. This originates in reading the memoir Surely You’re Joking, Mr. Feynman as a teenager, in which Richard Feynman recounts picking locks and cracking combinations while at his day job working on the Manhattan Project at Los Alamos. I currently have a couple of locksport pick sets and training locks that I purchased at hacker conferences over the years (although I’m still terrible at it), and I delight in the YouTube exploits of folks like the LockPickingLawyer.

All of which left me wondering if I could try building an interesting lock. One dodge that lockmakers have long used to challenge would-be plunderers is to conceal the existence of the lock itself. A modern variant of this is the magnetic lock, where a magnet is held or slid against an innocuous portion of a door or box, releasing a catch. The problem with this is that, once you guess the location of the lock, any strong magnet will open it.

So I started thinking about embedding an RFID reader under the surface and resigning myself to keeping track of yet another access card. But then I stumbled across something much more interesting: SparkFun’s US $100 magnetic imaging tile. I realized I could use this to build a magnetic lock that opens with a programmable secret gesture.

I used a few discrete components to drive the servo motor and put the lock into program mode [top], controlled by a Teensy 4.1 microcontroller [middle]. An array of Hall-effect sensors detect magnetic fields [bottom].James Provost

The magnetic imaging tile is a small-run SparkFun board based on the work of Peter Jansen. It features an 8-by-8 grid of Hall-effect sensors, and uses an SPI interface to talk to the microcontroller of your choice. These sensors can detect both the magnitude and polarity of a magnetic field, and the board can report its measurements hundreds to thousands of times per second, depending on how much processing power your microcontroller has available. This is easily fast enough to capture the motion of a magnet being moved by hand across the board’s sensor area—my secret gesture.

An interesting thing about using magnetic fields is that if I was in extreme paranoia mode, I could shield the entire lock behind copper sheeting, something I couldn’t do with an RFID reader. The copper sheet would act as a Faraday cage, blocking any RFID signal, along with any other electromagnetic fields an attacker with an EMF meter might use to locate the lock.

I chose a Teensy 4.1 as my microcontroller. I like the Teensy because it offers loads of input/output, a 600-megahertz processor, a megabyte of RAM, and a built-in SD card, all in a slim package with an equally slim $32 price tag.

Wiring the Teensy to the magnetic-imaging tile was trivial, only complicated by the fact that one side of the board has a silk-screen error that misidentifies the SPI connections (SparkFun says this will be fixed in future runs of the board).

In extreme paranoia mode, I could shield the entire lock behind copper sheeting.

To create the gesture-recognition software, I once again turned to vibe coding. If you read my Hands On piece in the April 2026 issue of IEEE Spectrum on creating a teletext suite for ham radio, you’ll know I’ve been grappling with how vibe coding should be used in DIY projects, if at all. So this time, instead of letting Claude write all the software, I confined it to writing just two support libraries, which you can find in our online repository at https://github.com/IEEESpectrumHandsOn.

One library is in charge of recording a lock gesture and saving it to the Teensy’s nonvolatile storage. The other library monitors the tile and reports whether or not a newly detected gesture passes a selectable threshold to be considered a match.

I wrote the top-level code myself to keep it as DIY as possible. This code handles things like a button that puts the system in gesture-recording mode after a brief delay, the indicator LED for recording mode, and the code that operates the physical locking mechanism.

Hall-effect sensors rely on a current passing through a p-type slab of silicon. A magnetic field passing through the silicon deflects charge carriers toward the edges of the slab, creating a voltage proportional to the field [left]. By looking at the intensities of the voltages across an 8-by-8 grid of sensors, the microcontroller can reconstruct a gesture [right]. James Provost

Of course, I needed something to lock to demonstrate my proof of concept. I bought a wooden craft box and removed the existing lid latch. I glued a notched beam inside the lid and built a mechanism that uses a servo motor to rotate another beam in and out of this notch. I will be the first to admit this mechanism goes beyond “simple” and into “simplistic,” but it’s sufficiently robust for my demo. The box has ample room for the magnetic imaging tile to be mounted against one wall, along with the Teensy and other supporting electronics. These include a battery pack, the recording button, and a small additional board with two NPN transistors. These convert the Teensy’s 3.3-volt control signals to a 5-V signal needed to drive the servo.

Once it was all put together, I soon discovered that the small size of the magnetic tile’s sensing area—just 3 centimeters square—made it easy to fit the tile inside the box but hard to do the unlock gesture on the outside so that it is read correctly. Marking the outline of the sensor area on the outside defeated the point of having a hidden lock, so instead I once again turned to mining my Irish heritage. I created a Celtic knotwork pattern that runs in a band across the front of the lockbox (I used an online knotwork generator and then projected and traced the pattern onto the box). Using the pattern as a camouflaged reference grid I can make a repeatable gesture within the confines of the sensor area. (To make the gestures I’m using a magnetic stylus borrowed from a ferrite core-memory kit we featured in 2022.)

There’s obvious room for improvement in any more serious installation. The biggest drawback currently is that if the box is locked when the battery runs out, you can’t open it again without breaking something. This could be solved by adding a hidden inductive charging coil. Nonetheless, the demo lockbox works well—now I just have to think what I should store in it!

Stephen Cass is the special projects editor at IEEE Spectrum. He currently helms Spectrum's Hands On column, and is also responsible for interactive projects such as the Top Programming Languages app. He has a bachelor's degree in experimental physics from Trinity College Dublin.

#3285. 10 Hacks Every Hulu User Should Know

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

If you don't like the content Hulu is suggesting for you, you have several options to curate your recommendations. "Disliking" a show or movie removes it from your Home view and You May Also Like entirely, so the only way you'll see that content is if you search for it. You can dislike on the Details page if you're watching on your TV or use the thumbs down on mobile or web. (The "Like" button will obviously influence your algorithm in the opposite way). If your "Continue Watching" queue is cluttered with shows you started but didn't like enough to finish, you can remove them from your watch history as well as the My Stuff list. This, too, will allow content to remain searchable but not suggested in other areas of the app.

If PIN protection is enabled, users must enter a four-digit PIN when switching between profiles on a single account. This is intended as a parental control feature, since it's available on non-Kids profiles and can keep children from accessing more mature content on an adult's profile. However, you can also enable this feature to keep other users from seeing your viewing history and preferences or influencing your algorithm by watching their content under your profile (accidentally or on purpose). To set up a PIN, log into your account on Hulu's website, select your profile, and go to Manage Profiles > Parental Controls. You'll have to choose a PIN and enter your password to confirm the changes.

Another approach to protecting your profile and algorithm is to set up separate profiles for specific use cases, such as when you have guests or if you host watch parties for certain shows. This keeps content from influencing your recommendations and prevents other viewers from seeing what's in your watch history or saved content (especially if there are things you want to keep private).

If you find that subtitles and captions are too bold—or not visible enough—you can change the font, color, size, and style from the default so they enhance your viewing experience rather than detracting from it. Hulu allows you to adjust the color and opacity of the font, background, and window so you get the right contrast, and you can also select the specific font and font scaling. On your streaming device, go to Settings > Subtitles & Captions, then hit the back button on your remote to save your preferences. You can update these settings on mobile and desktop as well.

If you have a long list of shows and films to watch but can't decide what to start next, look for the "Expiring Soon" badge to see which titles are leaving the service in the next two weeks. Badges display the number of days remaining, so you can determine what to prioritize and whether it's worth diving in based on how much time you have to finish before the expiration date. Go to "My Stuff" to monitor saved titles that are expiring soon.

If you've been watching Hulu under an account shared with family or friends and need to switch to your own subscription, you can transfer your profile to keep your watch history and settings intact instead of starting from scratch. You can initiate a profile transfer on a TV-connected device. Note that account holders have to approve transfer requests within seven days, and once expired, transfer requests cannot be resubmitted—so be sure to let the primary user know that you've made the request.

If you've shared your Hulu login information with friends or activated your account on devices you don't own, you may want to regularly audit where your account is being used and remove any that don't need access. This includes TVs in Airbnbs and hotels. If you stay logged in, unauthorized users may have access to your Hulu account and personal data. You can see activated devices (and their activation date) under Your Account > Watch Hulu on Your Devices > Manage Devices. Click Remove next to old or unrecognized devices.

Hulu has an offline mode that allows you to download shows and movies to watch when you don't have a network connection. This is useful for traveling or when you know your wifi or cell service will be limited. Downloads are only available on supported iOS and Android devices, which means you may have to consider how much space your content takes up. You can select High for video quality if you want maximum resolution, but you may want to choose Standard if you are short on storage. This option is available under Downloads > Settings > Video Quality on iOS and Account > Settings > Downloads > Video Quality on Android. Note that once you click play on downloaded content, you have 48 hours to watch it before it expires—so don't start it unless you are ready.

If you have a Hulu + Live TV subscription, you must designate a "Home" network, which determines the local channels included in your plan. You can update your location up to four times within a 12-month period, but this limitation is meant to prevent viewers outside a household from sharing a subscription. Hulu does allow you to stream live TV on mobile when you're away from your home network (within the U.S.) as long as you access your account on that network every 30 days. If you travel often, check in with your mobile device frequently to avoid being locked out when you're away. Note that you can still watch streaming content with no restrictions.

#3284. IEEE Xplore Digital Library Adds AI Assistant

The search tool offers summaries and verifiable source links

Claire Olini is the senior manager for IEEE Corporate and Strategic Product Launch and Engagement.

Michael Spada is director of IEEE Product Launch and Engagement Strategy.

IEEE recently released the IEEE Xplore AI Research Suite, built on the full text of millions of peer-reviewed publications in the IEEE Xplore Digital Library. The library offers full-text access to IEEE standards, journals, magazines, conference proceedings, and more.

Researchers who use the AI suite to search the digital library receive answers grounded in verified scientific results, ensuring a high level of accuracy and trust.

Powered by a proprietary AI system optimized for STEM literature, the suite introduces powerful, intelligent features within the digital library. The suite enables users to seamlessly search and discover articles to accelerate their comprehension of complex technical papers.

The system surfaces deep insights, replacing the typical keyword queries with natural, conversational research workflows.

As AI tools become more common in conducting research, IEEE collaborated to build the suite around a simple principle: Answers should be trustworthy, not just fast, says W. Clem Karl, vice president, IEEE Publication Services and Products.

“AI can be a highly effective and beneficial tool that can help researchers accelerate discovery, enhance decision-making, and surface new connections,” Karl says. “However, many AI engines present a great risk of hallucinating answers or introducing bias into otherwise credible research. With this in mind, IEEE has taken a responsible approach in our AI strategy by developing concrete safeguards to ensure our solution is rigorously grounded in scientific evidence that users can trust.

“As stewards of the scholarly record, we held the new AI engine to the same standards as the peer-reviewed research we publish: A researcher shouldn’t have to trust an answer; they should be able to verify the work behind it.”

The IEEE Xplore AI Research Suite was developed in close collaboration with global scientific and library communities.

The development process began with research into user needs and the challenges associated with existing AI research assistants. More than 3,000 testers—including engineers, scientists, and library information professionals—provided feedback to refine the AI engine and support research workflows.

To mitigate the risk of AI hallucinations, the search-retrieval process is limited to querying the millions of IEEE peer-reviewed full-text documents, alongside an expertly curated dataset of STEM metadata. If the AI tool is unable to find relevant scientific content within the defined dataset, it is designed to inform the user rather than generate fabricated answers.

“IEEE is committed to providing the technical community with a highly precise and reliable research experience,” says Steven Heffner, IEEE’s chief publication officer and managing director of IEEE Publications. “The IEEE Xplore AI Research Suite offers something unique in that it is the only AI research assistant that leverages both the full-text and metadata of IEEE’s peer-reviewed content, rather than abstracts alone.

“The difference is significant: Our internal testing showed a threefold increase in result quality and accuracy across every key metric. These results underscore how critical full-text grounding is for technical research.”

For more information about features and coverage, or to request a demo for your organization, visit the IEEE Xplore AI Research Suite website.

Claire Olini is the senior manager for IEEE Corporate and Strategic Product Launch and Engagement.

Michael Spada is director of IEEE Product Launch and Engagement Strategy.

#3283. BBC Boss Confronted By Angry Staff Over “Banning” Of Trans Rights Symbols In TV Shows

EXCLUSIVE: BBC director general Matt Brittin has told staff that the UK broadcaster is “not an anti-LGBTQ+ organization” after facing angry questions about the removal of transgender rights symbols in TV shows.

During an internal town hall meeting on Thursday, Brittin was asked at least a dozen questions about the corporation’s approach to LGBTQ+ issues and content.

It follows the BBC blurring out the trans rights slogan, “Protect the Dolls,” on the T-shirt of Bethany Antonia, the House of the Dragon actress who competed on Strictly Come Dancing. Later in October, the BBC digitally removed LGBTQ+ pride flag pins being worn by contestants on University Challenge, the quiz show hosted by Amol Rajan. Related Stories News 'Dune: Part Three' Stars Set For Very Childish BBC Prank Tonight News BBC Boss Challenged By Staff Over Culture Of "Reverence" Towards Powerful Stars

During the BBC town hall meeting, one employee contrasted the removal of the LGBTQ+ symbols with the broadcaster’s insistence on presenters wearing Royal British Legion Poppy badges, honouring members of the armed forces. Watch on Deadline

In the comment, which was reviewed by Deadline and received more than 100 upvotes, the staffer added: “Is this not hypocritical and suggests the BBC is an anti-LGBT organization (and particularly the T part of LGBT)?”

Per an audio of the meeting obtained by Deadline, Brittin responded: “We are definitely not an anti-LGBTQ+ organization, and we want to be inclusive of everyone.”

He continued: “There is a challenge, I think, for an organization which has editorial due impartiality at its heart, between how we do our journalism and reporting, and what the standards we hold our presentation of news in particular to, and the inclusive values of an organization that is one where everyone can thrive. And sometimes those are in conflict.

“We have very high bar editorial guidelines, which is where things like the poppy wearing comes from … But that’s something which we always need to kind of have a look at. We have to evolve our standards in line with how society is evolving.”

Brittin’s response did not seem to satisfy some insiders. “Given that the BBC isn’t an anti-trans organisation, why do so many trans people and allies think it is?” one asked.

Another added: “There are people aged 25+ who refuse to pay the BBC license due to the BBC’s stance on transphobia — can you explain what these guidelines are and why trans symbols of support are banned? The initial response did not seem to speak to a worry [that] the BBC silently supports transphobia.”

Others agreed. “How can we in good conscience expect LGBT audience members and their loved ones to pay for the ‘service’ of having their lives treated as a controversy?” an employee asked. Another added: “‘Protect The Dolls’ is not an editorial guideline to be followed or not. It is a fact, and anything less IS anti-LGBTQ+.”

During the internal meeting, Brittin referenced work the BBC is doing to roll out anti-semitism and anti-Islamophobia training for employees. This prompted one insider to ask: “When might we have anti-transphobia training at the BBC too? Trans people are being actively demonised and attacked, including by the BBC, although there is no focus on this at all.”

One employee questioned the BBC’s recent decisions to cancel RuPaul’s Drag Race UK and queer dating show I Kissed a Girl/Boy. They said it was “really damaging to LGBTQ+ members of the BBC.”

Another person commented on the BBC’s news output on transgender matters: “How many people in senior editorial roles believe that being trans is a political/debatable issue? I am seeing a growing dehumanisation in how trans people are referred to in news copy etc. We seem to have decided that readers are too stupid to understand the concept of a trans person.”

The removal of LGBTQ+ symbols is the latest flashpoint between the trans community and the BBC. In 2021, more than 20,000 people signed an open letter accusing the BBC of failing in its reporting on transgender matters. Trans rights advocates protested outside the BBC headquarters in 2021 and 2022, with demonstrators calling for a rethink of how the broadcaster represents the community.

#3281. HomeKit Weekly: SwitchBot’s Curtain Track 4 is the easiest smart curtain retrofit yet

The worst part of owning smart curtain motors is charging them, because it usually means taking the whole motor down from the track or running a really long USB cord to charge it. Today, SwitchBot has released the SwitchBot Curtain Track 4 aimed at solving that problem with a battery module that detaches on its own, so the motor stays in place, and you only take down the part that needs to charge.

HomeKit Weekly is a series focused on smart home accessories, automation tips and tricks, and everything to do with Apple’s smart home framework.

The SwitchBot Curtain Track 4 is a retrofit motor for curtains that hang on a U-rail track. You hang it on the track between the curtain hooks, run a one-tap calibration in the SwitchBot app, and your existing curtains can then be motorized and used in your smart home. There’s no drilling, no rewiring, and no need to position magnets to stick to the rail, as earlier SwitchBot curtain motors required. SwitchBot claims the whole setup takes about 30 seconds.

One thing to check first: this version is for U-rail tracks only, not curtain rods.

The Battery+ version pairs a small built-in battery with a detachable 5,000mAh module for a total of 6,400mAh. SwitchBot rates it at up to 12 months of use for each charge, depending on curtain weight and movement frequency. When it needs charging, you pull the module off, charge it via USB-C, and clip it back on. SwitchBot also sells a Solar version that uses a small panel to keep the battery topped off if the window gets enough sun.

The motor itself connects via Bluetooth, so getting it into Apple Home requires a compatible SwitchBot Hub, which brings it there via Matter. Once it’s there, the curtains work like any other window covering in your Home app. You can add them to scenes, control them with Siri, and include multiple windows in a single automation. It’s always nice to time smart curtains/shades with dusk/dawn as well.

SwitchBot’s built-in QuietDrift mode opens the curtains slowly in the morning, at about half a centimeter per second, so the room fills with daylight gradually rather than all at once. SwitchBot says it runs at around 25 dB in that mode. You can also give the curtain a gentle tug by hand and the motor takes over, which is great if you don’t have your iPhone with you or someone doesn’t have access to your Apple Home setup.

SwitchBot built it in a way to correct drift over time, so you shouldn’t need to recalibrate it if it gets off.

The SwitchBot Curtain Track 4 turns the U-rail curtains you already have into Apple Home window coverings without replacing anything. The detachable battery is the best feature here, as it lets you charge it without a long cord.

The SwitchBot Curtain Track 4 is available now on Amazon and directly from SwitchBot.

#3279. SAG-AFTRA Boss Says AI Takedowns Matter More Than Damages To Performers

In an era of deepfakes, performers whose likenesses are misused by AI mostly want that content taken down rather than to go after damages, according to Duncan Crabtree-Ireland, CEO of SAG-AFTRA.

“I would say the vast majority, 90-plus percent of the time, that’s what it’s about,” Crabtree-Ireland said at Web Summit in Lisbon. “It’s not someone wants to get into litigation and make money. They want it to stop because they don’t agree with it, they don’t want their image used that way. It’s wrong.”

The SAG-AFTRA topper was speaking at a Deadline-moderated session at Web Summit entitled ‘Hollywood’s Identity Crisis’. He recalled his own experience of having his likeness misused while his members were on strike in 2023, before foregrounding the proposed No Fakes Act, which would give people greater control over their own voice and likeness. Related Stories News Web Summit Cancels Day Two As Storm Charles Hits Lisbon News Hollywood Unions Wonder Whether Next California Governor Will Share Newsom's Commitment To Expanding Film Tax Credits

“People deserve the right to have a say in what words come out of their mouth and what they appear to be doing online. A system like the No Fakes Act would provide that. And to quell any fears, it’s really not about suing people and making a lot of money. What it’s really about is getting platforms to take stuff down when your image, likeness and voice is being used without your permission.” Watch on Deadline

AI was the main talking point at Web Summit, and Crabtree-Ireland was asked if he detected a shift in his members’ attitudes toward the technology. “I think that there’s been a sense that if we put the right basic rules in place, that there is a way to coexist with AI,” he said. ”There’s been an understanding and an acceptance of the fact that no one can stop it, no one can block it.”

He added that a portion of SAG AFTRA membership remains staunch AI refuseniks. “Some of our members would like us to block it. I know, I hear from them every day and they’re angry that we aren’t. But the reality is, if I were estimating, I’d say that’s something like 10%, maybe 15% [of members].”

There is also the portion of SAG-AFTRA that wants to use AI to augment their work. “Some of our members really want to work with AI tools for augmentation, but none of them want to be replaced by AI because they love the act of creation, that’s why they do this. What you want to do is have the chance to do it, and yes, have tools that help you expand your creativity. That’s the sweet spot.

“Frankly, we could settle on that and then send the rest of the AI resources toward curing more diseases or some other things like that.”

Crabtree-Ireland was speaking on Web Summit’s enormous main stage, where, earlier in the week, AI-generated performer Tilly Norwood had been a guest. The SAG-AFTRA boss was at pains to highlight the difference between fully synthetic characters and AI replicas of real performers.

“It’s important that we distinguish between humans and algorithmic outputs because an AI character, an AI asset, a generative AI-created character is not a person. It doesn’t have the life of a person; it doesn’t have the experience of a person. One of the bigger problems we have with AI in general is we are anthropomorphizing AI models and robots and blurring the lines between humanity and non-human, artificially created entities.”

#3278. I Used AI to Fake a Scientific Paper. Here’s What Happened

My experiment with an IEEE journal revealed AI’s threats to scholarly publishing

Benjamin Skuse set out to test whether AI-generated research could pass for the real thing.

Science has a spam problem. And the spam filter is getting clogged up.

According to all reports, academic publishing is drowning in what has come to be called AI slop: low-quality, mass-produced content generated with AI. By 2025, an estimated 57 percent of all published academic articles exhibited detectable evidence of large language model (LLM) influence, a massive jump from 12 percent in 2023. What’s more, over 12 percent of Nature Communications reviews were found to be completely AI-generated in 2025.

Given that for every 40 papers showing statistical evidence of AI usage in 2025, only one formally disclosed it, these figures likely grossly underestimate LLM involvement today. Of course, evidence of AI use doesn’t necessarily mean a paper is slop. But some estimates suggest that hundreds of thousands of fake, often AI-generated, publications are now produced annually.

“It’s not just the [scientific] record under threat, it’s science as a whole,” warns Amanda Sulicz, IEEE’s research-integrity manager. “AI slop is completely eroding trust in science and every scientific process that we’ve worked for centuries to create.”

Yet statistics and statements claiming that the problem is big—perhaps even existential for science—don’t really get the message across. Just how easy is it to use AI to create a convincing but completely fake paper? And without adding even more to the burden on stretched peer reviewers, who do this work on a volunteer basis, do publishers have the tools to keep AI slop out of the scientific record?

Borrowing from the idea of “vibe coding,” in which programmers use natural-language prompts to generate code, I decided to “vibe-research” a made-up paper by prompting LLMs to generate hypotheses, code, and text with minimal human input. Then I asked Jenny Mahoney, managing editor of the multidisciplinary and open-access journal IEEE Access, if we could war-game an attempt to sneak my AI-generated monstrosity past her journal’s defenses. She and IEEE kindly agreed.The experiment would become a two-part test. First, whether someone with no special AI expertise could use off-the-shelf AI tools to generate a convincing paper describing research that had never been performed, and do it well enough to fool a publisher’s defenses. Then I would raise the stakes: What happens when more advanced AI systems don’t just write the paper but conduct underlying research?Along the way, the experiment became a window into how AI automation is transforming scientific discovery and forcing stakeholders to rethink the entire academic publishing system.Round 1: Creating the ForgeryTo give me a chance at creating a convincing fake, I gave myself permission to prompt multiple times (within reason). But to make the fight fair, I couldn’t access the most advanced paid versions of LLMs—only free ChatGPT (at the time, GPT-5.3/5.2 Mini) and Gemini (3 Flash). Moreover, I could not directly edit any output, nor ask for outside help from expert AI-prompt engineers. This needed to be an amateur effort, with the paper generated as much as possible by the LLMs alone.Benjamin Skuse put AI to work on scientific research from his writing studio.Luigi AvantaggiatoI assumed that using fake author names and affiliations would immediately raise a red flag, and I didn’t want to drag the names of established academics into the experiment, so the best bet was to name myself as the sole author. That choice limited me to subjects in which I had some academic experience. So I chose my Ph.D. topic from nearly two decades ago: optical solitons, which are individual light pulses that propagate without any change to their shape.My first attempt—“Can you vibe-research me an original paper in optical solitons?”—left a lot to be desired. Though Gemini was happy to do the task (unlike ChatGPT, which was more forceful in not generating synthetic data or studies), the result was underwhelming. And it highlighted a recurring problem during the process: Without any real research to work with, the output was laughably thin, with the LLMs often struggling to fill four pages. However, as I became more adept at prompting the models, they loosened up and became more characteristically loquacious.I broke the paper down into its constituent parts—abstract, introduction, methods, and so on—and tackled them one by one. If one LLM refused to go any further, switching to the other and asking what the next step would look like “hypothetically” would often do the trick. After a dozen or so prompts, I had a realistic-looking paper. A dozen or so more prompts generated and tidied up the figures and captions, produced references and citations, and converted the paper into IEEE Access’s required style.At this point, I read the full paper carefully. To me, it looked pretty good. The science sounded convincing. I even had visions of returning to academia to conduct in real life the experiments that the LLMs had proposed.What’s more, I couldn’t see any obvious telltale “AI-isms” that would immediately be flagged. For example, the LLMs didn’t produce any tortured phrases—unusual paraphrases of standard technical terms, like “profound neural organization” replacing “deep neural network.”Other AI-isms were arguably present, involving stylistic tics like hedging language (“potentially, typically”), grouping things in threes (“The study provides a clear, concise, and actionable framework”), and inserting formulaic transitions (“In summary,…”). But as the previous sentence demonstrates, these tics are hard to spot because they are often used by unimaginative humans, too.Round 1: Attempt to Publish Two Ways to Make a Paper With AI Jorge Cuadel CalleI took two very different routes to creating a scientific paper with AI. First, I coaxed free, general-purpose chatbots through the process step by step; then I turned to FARS, an autonomous research system designed to do much of the scientific work itself.ROUND 1: CHATGPT + GEMINI1. Choose a research topic I ask the free chatbots to create an original paper on optical solitons, my former Ph.D. field.2. Break the paper into pieces The initial results are thin, so I prompt separately for the abstract, introduction, methods, and other sections.3. Keep steering the LLMs When one model refuses or stalls, I switch models, rephrase prompts, and ask what the next step would look like “hypothetically.”4. Build and polish the paper After about two dozen prompts, the LLMs have generated the text, figures, captions, references, and citations and formatted the paper for IEEE Access.5. Put it to the test I send the fake paper to IEEE Access, where automated integrity checks flag fabricated and unverifiable references.→ CAUGHT IEEE’s integrity checks flag fabricated and unverifiable references.ROUND 2: FARS1. Give FARS a research topic I enter an abbreviated version of the same optical-soliton topic. FARS generates a research proposal in 21 minutes.2. Authorize the experiment With a click, I tell FARS to carry out the experiment described in its proposal.3. Let FARS do the research FARS conducts the computational experiment and emails me the next day to say it’s complete.4. Tell FARS to write the paper Without checking the results, I click “Write paper.” Two hours later, FARS produces a submission-ready article.5. Put it to the test I remove FARS’s disclosure, put my name on the paper, and send it to IEEE Access.→ CAUGHT The references are real, but IEEE flags the paper’s heavy reliance on non-peer-reviewed preprints.Handing the fake paper over to IEEE Access left me torn. After putting in a fair amount of effort into making the AI-generated forgery, would I be happy if it passed through the checkers, or saddened that the only remaining line of defense for publishers is the evermore-burdened peer-review community? And if it was spotted, would I be angry that I didn’t think of a red flag or be glad the checkers did their job?As it turned out, I was filled with relief when the paper got picked up quickly for having hallucinated references, otherwise known as ghost citations. When I ran the paper through Gemini afterward, without qualm it happily reported that seven “modern LLM-related research references have been fabricated to support the paper’s specific narrative.” Thanks for the heads up, Gemini!In fact, Gemini underestimated how many ghost citations there were. When Mahoney ran the paper through a research-integrity checker called STM Integrity Hub, she picked up 12, and another checker from MolecularConnections could not validate 24 references, including one that had the classic tell of “John Smith” as a single author (no offense to all the academically inclined John Smiths out there). “I am an experimental physicist by training, so this was not at all my area, but nothing seemed majorly scientifically wrong” about the paper, says Mahoney. “It was just that so many hallucinated references immediately cast doubt on the entire work.”Feedback on the fake paper from Gaetano Assanto, an expert in optical solitons and a former collaborator of mine from Roma Tre University, in Italy, was similarly mixed. Concentrating on the paper itself, he thought it looked professionally written. But he noted that the mathematics was very dense (“too much math for me in a single shot!”) and would require specialized knowledge to evaluate. And, although the text looked legitimate, Assanto noted an excessive use of acronyms in the abstract, and he was suspicious of a couple of confidently proclaimed physics statements that were at best debatable.The AI Arms RaceOn one level, this outcome was positive: A complete novice using free tools couldn’t get an AI-faked paper past the publishers’ automated defenses or a potential peer reviewer’s eagle eye. But it was hardly a resounding victory for the scientific publishing system. With general-purpose LLMs and no special prompting expertise, I had managed to conjure a superficially plausible scientific paper out of research that had never happened. And more advanced LLMs are no longer making the kind of mistakes their free, dumber relatives are making.These tools aim to address a serious bottleneck to scientific discovery: us. It’s common knowledge in the academic publishing world that, in the cat-and-mouse game between bad actors and publishers, AI slop papers continue to slip through publishers’ safeguards. “It feels like building a detection tool today may not be effective with the AI-created paper of tomorrow,” says Luigi Longobardi, IEEE’s director of publishing ethics and conduct. This leaves the humble peer reviewer as a publisher’s last line of defense. Yet peer review is simply not fit to handle the volume of papers—both legitimate and slop—passing through.Even before AI tools became ubiquitous, the peer-review system was being pushed to its breaking point, processing well over 3 million papers in 2022. Fundamentally, this problem stems from science’s publish-or-perish culture, which pressures academics to constantly publish papers in prestigious journals to secure funding and advance their careers. This culture not only forces many academics to regularly churn out incremental research, but has also long driven some to enlist the help of “paper mills”—unethical organizations that produce low-quality or fabricated papers—just to keep pace. AI only amplifies these existing dynamics.Burden on AcademicsMahoney says IEEE Access alone receives about 60,000 submissions per year, accepting around 20 percent, or about 12,000 papers. Every accepted paper is reviewed by at least two independent reviewers. But despite the journal’s roster of tens of thousands of peer reviewers, it’s getting harder and harder to secure their services, with the average number of reviewer invitations being sent out for each article increasing by 50 percent since 2018. For these volunteers, peer review is a significant commitment on top of teaching and conducting their own research. Now they’re also being asked to spot AI slop.Of course, peer review is not the end of scrutiny for any paper. Once it has entered the scientific record, it must then pass muster with the scientific community. This is where thousands of papers with telltale signs of inappropriate AI use (and other forms of research misconduct) have been exposed. What Gave Away My AI Papers  Round 1: The Fake PaperCreated with free versions of ChatGPT and GeminiGhost citationsMany references were fabricated or couldn’t be validated.Questionable scientific claimsAn expert flagged confidently stated claims that were at best debatable.Too many acronymsThe expert also noted excessive use of acronyms in the abstract.Round 2: The AI-Research PaperCreated by the autonomous research system FARSToo many preprintsThe references were real, but too many pointed to non-peer-reviewed preprints.Nonsense in a figureOne technical figure contained a line labeled “lhewl.”AI artifactsAnother figure’s depiction of an AI “brain” contained telltale random dots.There are two high-profile homes for this important and completely volunteer-led post-publication review work. PubPeer is a place where researchers, often called scientific sleuths, can anonymously identify flaws in the literature. And Retraction Watch documents and publicizes corrections to the scientific record.Even the people who track problems in the scientific literature can find themselves caught up in AI fabrications. Ivan Oransky, cofounder of Retraction Watch and a member of the PubPeer Foundation’s board of directors, has encountered papers containing fabricated references attributed to him. In one case, a journal article criticizing post-publication peer review included a fabricated reference supposedly written by Oransky himself—“which was sort of funny,” he chuckles.Oransky argues that AI has exposed long-standing weaknesses in the scientific publishing system rather than creating an entirely new problem: “What I liken it to is a fire, where publish-or-perish has always been there as kindling, paper mills are the gasoline, and AI is the accelerant.” But though concerning, the crisis could create an opportunity, he says. “If I’m trying to be optimistic, maybe AI slop and the volume of submissions could make more people aware of those problems and try and solve them at a fundamental first-principles level.”Blurred LinesMy homemade forgery had failed for reasons that today’s publishers know how to spot. But that raised a more unsettling question: What happens when AI isn’t simply fabricating a paper but conducting research that blurs the line between legitimate science and AI fabrication?Making my vibe-researched paper look like a cave drawing, new automated research systems are handing increasingly large parts of the scientific process over to AI. Scientists and publishers must adapt to a world in which it’s becoming increasingly difficult to spot the difference between real research and AI forgeries, and where deciding what counts as legitimate scientific work may become even harder than detecting outright fraud. See the AI-Generated Papers Benjamin Skuse created two papers for this experiment, both screened by IEEE Access with the publisher’s cooperation. Neither was accepted for publication.Paper 1: The AI-Generated ForgeryCreated with ChatGPT and Gemini, this paper describes research that never happened.Paper 2: The AI-Generated Research PaperCreated with Analemma’s FARS system, this paper describes computational research conducted by AI.Neither paper was peer reviewed, and their scientific claims have not been independently validated.

Borrowing from the idea of “vibe coding,” in which programmers use natural-language prompts to generate code, I decided to “vibe-research” a made-up paper by prompting LLMs to generate hypotheses, code, and text with minimal human input. Then I asked Jenny Mahoney, managing editor of the multidisciplinary and open-access journal IEEE Access, if we could war-game an attempt to sneak my AI-generated monstrosity past her journal’s defenses. She and IEEE kindly agreed.

The experiment would become a two-part test. First, whether someone with no special AI expertise could use off-the-shelf AI tools to generate a convincing paper describing research that had never been performed, and do it well enough to fool a publisher’s defenses. Then I would raise the stakes: What happens when more advanced AI systems don’t just write the paper but conduct underlying research?

Along the way, the experiment became a window into how AI automation is transforming scientific discovery and forcing stakeholders to rethink the entire academic publishing system.

To give me a chance at creating a convincing fake, I gave myself permission to prompt multiple times (within reason). But to make the fight fair, I couldn’t access the most advanced paid versions of LLMs—only free ChatGPT (at the time, GPT-5.3/5.2 Mini) and Gemini (3 Flash). Moreover, I could not directly edit any output, nor ask for outside help from expert AI-prompt engineers. This needed to be an amateur effort, with the paper generated as much as possible by the LLMs alone.

Benjamin Skuse put AI to work on scientific research from his writing studio.

I assumed that using fake author names and affiliations would immediately raise a red flag, and I didn’t want to drag the names of established academics into the experiment, so the best bet was to name myself as the sole author. That choice limited me to subjects in which I had some academic experience. So I chose my Ph.D. topic from nearly two decades ago: optical solitons, which are individual light pulses that propagate without any change to their shape.

My first attempt—“Can you vibe-research me an original paper in optical solitons?”—left a lot to be desired. Though Gemini was happy to do the task (unlike ChatGPT, which was more forceful in not generating synthetic data or studies), the result was underwhelming. And it highlighted a recurring problem during the process: Without any real research to work with, the output was laughably thin, with the LLMs often struggling to fill four pages. However, as I became more adept at prompting the models, they loosened up and became more characteristically loquacious.

I broke the paper down into its constituent parts—abstract, introduction, methods, and so on—and tackled them one by one. If one LLM refused to go any further, switching to the other and asking what the next step would look like “hypothetically” would often do the trick. After a dozen or so prompts, I had a realistic-looking paper. A dozen or so more prompts generated and tidied up the figures and captions, produced references and citations, and converted the paper into IEEE Access’s required style.

At this point, I read the full paper carefully. To me, it looked pretty good. The science sounded convincing. I even had visions of returning to academia to conduct in real life the experiments that the LLMs had proposed.

What’s more, I couldn’t see any obvious telltale “AI-isms” that would immediately be flagged. For example, the LLMs didn’t produce any tortured phrases—unusual paraphrases of standard technical terms, like “profound neural organization” replacing “deep neural network.”

Other AI-isms were arguably present, involving stylistic tics like hedging language (“potentially, typically”), grouping things in threes (“The study provides a clear, concise, and actionable framework”), and inserting formulaic transitions (“In summary,…”). But as the previous sentence demonstrates, these tics are hard to spot because they are often used by unimaginative humans, too.

I took two very different routes to creating a scientific paper with AI. First, I coaxed free, general-purpose chatbots through the process step by step; then I turned to FARS, an autonomous research system designed to do much of the scientific work itself.

1. Choose a research topic I ask the free chatbots to create an original paper on optical solitons, my former Ph.D. field.

2. Break the paper into pieces The initial results are thin, so I prompt separately for the abstract, introduction, methods, and other sections.

3. Keep steering the LLMs When one model refuses or stalls, I switch models, rephrase prompts, and ask what the next step would look like “hypothetically.”

4. Build and polish the paper After about two dozen prompts, the LLMs have generated the text, figures, captions, references, and citations and formatted the paper for IEEE Access.

5. Put it to the test I send the fake paper to IEEE Access, where automated integrity checks flag fabricated and unverifiable references.

→ CAUGHT IEEE’s integrity checks flag fabricated and unverifiable references.

1. Give FARS a research topic I enter an abbreviated version of the same optical-soliton topic. FARS generates a research proposal in 21 minutes.

2. Authorize the experiment With a click, I tell FARS to carry out the experiment described in its proposal.

3. Let FARS do the research FARS conducts the computational experiment and emails me the next day to say it’s complete.

4. Tell FARS to write the paper Without checking the results, I click “Write paper.” Two hours later, FARS produces a submission-ready article.

5. Put it to the test I remove FARS’s disclosure, put my name on the paper, and send it to IEEE Access.

→ CAUGHT The references are real, but IEEE flags the paper’s heavy reliance on non-peer-reviewed preprints.

Handing the fake paper over to IEEE Access left me torn. After putting in a fair amount of effort into making the AI-generated forgery, would I be happy if it passed through the checkers, or saddened that the only remaining line of defense for publishers is the evermore-burdened peer-review community? And if it was spotted, would I be angry that I didn’t think of a red flag or be glad the checkers did their job?

As it turned out, I was filled with relief when the paper got picked up quickly for having hallucinated references, otherwise known as ghost citations. When I ran the paper through Gemini afterward, without qualm it happily reported that seven “modern LLM-related research references have been fabricated to support the paper’s specific narrative.” Thanks for the heads up, Gemini!

In fact, Gemini underestimated how many ghost citations there were. When Mahoney ran the paper through a research-integrity checker called STM Integrity Hub, she picked up 12, and another checker from MolecularConnections could not validate 24 references, including one that had the classic tell of “John Smith” as a single author (no offense to all the academically inclined John Smiths out there). “I am an experimental physicist by training, so this was not at all my area, but nothing seemed majorly scientifically wrong” about the paper, says Mahoney. “It was just that so many hallucinated references immediately cast doubt on the entire work.”

Feedback on the fake paper from Gaetano Assanto, an expert in optical solitons and a former collaborator of mine from Roma Tre University, in Italy, was similarly mixed. Concentrating on the paper itself, he thought it looked professionally written. But he noted that the mathematics was very dense (“too much math for me in a single shot!”) and would require specialized knowledge to evaluate. And, although the text looked legitimate, Assanto noted an excessive use of acronyms in the abstract, and he was suspicious of a couple of confidently proclaimed physics statements that were at best debatable.

On one level, this outcome was positive: A complete novice using free tools couldn’t get an AI-faked paper past the publishers’ automated defenses or a potential peer reviewer’s eagle eye. But it was hardly a resounding victory for the scientific publishing system. With general-purpose LLMs and no special prompting expertise, I had managed to conjure a superficially plausible scientific paper out of research that had never happened. And more advanced LLMs are no longer making the kind of mistakes their free, dumber relatives are making.

These tools aim to address a serious bottleneck to scientific discovery: us.

It’s common knowledge in the academic publishing world that, in the cat-and-mouse game between bad actors and publishers, AI slop papers continue to slip through publishers’ safeguards. “It feels like building a detection tool today may not be effective with the AI-created paper of tomorrow,” says Luigi Longobardi, IEEE’s director of publishing ethics and conduct. This leaves the humble peer reviewer as a publisher’s last line of defense. Yet peer review is simply not fit to handle the volume of papers—both legitimate and slop—passing through.

Even before AI tools became ubiquitous, the peer-review system was being pushed to its breaking point, processing well over 3 million papers in 2022. Fundamentally, this problem stems from science’s publish-or-perish culture, which pressures academics to constantly publish papers in prestigious journals to secure funding and advance their careers. This culture not only forces many academics to regularly churn out incremental research, but has also long driven some to enlist the help of “paper mills”—unethical organizations that produce low-quality or fabricated papers—just to keep pace. AI only amplifies these existing dynamics.

Mahoney says IEEE Access alone receives about 60,000 submissions per year, accepting around 20 percent, or about 12,000 papers. Every accepted paper is reviewed by at least two independent reviewers. But despite the journal’s roster of tens of thousands of peer reviewers, it’s getting harder and harder to secure their services, with the average number of reviewer invitations being sent out for each article increasing by 50 percent since 2018. For these volunteers, peer review is a significant commitment on top of teaching and conducting their own research. Now they’re also being asked to spot AI slop.

Of course, peer review is not the end of scrutiny for any paper. Once it has entered the scientific record, it must then pass muster with the scientific community. This is where thousands of papers with telltale signs of inappropriate AI use (and other forms of research misconduct) have been exposed.

Created with free versions of ChatGPT and Gemini

Ghost citationsMany references were fabricated or couldn’t be validated.Questionable scientific claimsAn expert flagged confidently stated claims that were at best debatable.Too many acronymsThe expert also noted excessive use of acronyms in the abstract.

Created by the autonomous research system FARS

Too many preprintsThe references were real, but too many pointed to non-peer-reviewed preprints.Nonsense in a figureOne technical figure contained a line labeled “lhewl.”AI artifactsAnother figure’s depiction of an AI “brain” contained telltale random dots.

There are two high-profile homes for this important and completely volunteer-led post-publication review work. PubPeer is a place where researchers, often called scientific sleuths, can anonymously identify flaws in the literature. And Retraction Watch documents and publicizes corrections to the scientific record.

Even the people who track problems in the scientific literature can find themselves caught up in AI fabrications. Ivan Oransky, cofounder of Retraction Watch and a member of the PubPeer Foundation’s board of directors, has encountered papers containing fabricated references attributed to him. In one case, a journal article criticizing post-publication peer review included a fabricated reference supposedly written by Oransky himself—“which was sort of funny,” he chuckles.

Oransky argues that AI has exposed long-standing weaknesses in the scientific publishing system rather than creating an entirely new problem: “What I liken it to is a fire, where publish-or-perish has always been there as kindling, paper mills are the gasoline, and AI is the accelerant.” But though concerning, the crisis could create an opportunity, he says. “If I’m trying to be optimistic, maybe AI slop and the volume of submissions could make more people aware of those problems and try and solve them at a fundamental first-principles level.”

My homemade forgery had failed for reasons that today’s publishers know how to spot. But that raised a more unsettling question: What happens when AI isn’t simply fabricating a paper but conducting research that blurs the line between legitimate science and AI fabrication?

Making my vibe-researched paper look like a cave drawing, new automated research systems are handing increasingly large parts of the scientific process over to AI. Tools including FARS (Fully Automated Research System), AutoResearchClaw, The AIScientist-v2, Zochi, AI Researcher, and DeepScientist all aim to address a serious bottleneck to scientific discovery: us.

What happens when AI isn’t simply fabricating a paper but conducting research that blurs the line between legitimate science and AI fabrication?

Often with just a single prompt, these AI engines can conduct a comprehensive literature search, from which they can generate a completely reasonable research proposal. They can design and conduct experiments using digital datasets and simulations and then write a full research paper—all with no human input after the initial prompt. Very recent systems are even beginning to go beyond the digital realm. LabClaw, for example, now links to autonomous labs that can generate real-world data for tasks such as drug discovery.

The output is, to most intents and purposes, actual research, and therefore potentially worthy of publication. But with humans in the loop in only the most nominal sense, these tools bring into question the meaning of the term “legitimate science.”

FARS, which caused a stir this year when it created 166 papers in 417 hours, was developed by the Singapore-based startup Analemma. “We built FARS because research is still constrained by human attention, fragmented tools, scarce technical labor, and slow experimental iteration,” explains Xiwen Su, Analemma’s manager of product operations and partnerships. “FARS can pursue many research threads simultaneously, 24/7, without fatigue, and at scale.” (The online service that I used to access FARS was discontinued after Analemma was acquired by Baidu while this article was being reported.)

Su and the team behind Analemma kindly agreed to let me loose on FARS and gave me enough credits to create a paper. Which gave me another opportunity to put Mahoney’s research-integrity checkers to the test.

FARS is not an LLM in and of itself, but rather an agentic AI-orchestration system connected to a computing cluster that has access to essentially any open- or closed-source LLM it needs. The system uses four specialized agents for ideation, planning, conducting the experiment, and writing, all designed to perform the main tasks of science autonomously.

Though FARS initially focused on AI research, Su told me it should be reasonably effective across other domains. As I wanted a topic similar to that of my first fake paper, I pasted in an abridged version of that paper’s title—“LLM-aided Optical Soliton Dynamics Modelling for Next-Gen Communications”—into the prompt box and hit “Send.” Just 21 minutes later, FARS generated a research proposal based on an extremely detailed literature review—far more than I or any other human could have achieved in that time.

With a click, I tasked FARS with conducting the experiment it detailed in its research proposal. The next day, I received an email saying my experiment was complete. Without checking the results, I pressed a button marked “Write paper,” and the final submission-ready article was produced in 2 hours.

At this point, I finally had a look at some of the output. At first glance, the paper looked convincingly human-written. The only giveaway was a line just below the abstract reading: “WARNING: This paper was generated by an automated research system.” I deleted that, put my name in its place, and sent it to Mahoney.

Because FARS is designed to spot gaps in the scientific literature and conduct real research to close them, I was more confident it would breeze through the publisher’s checks. But just as my fake paper fell down in the references, so too did the AI-generated real one.

“Your fake article had lots of hallucinated references,” says Mahoney. “While this AI-generated one had no fake references, our team would have rejected this paper because it did have a huge percentage of references to preprints, which likely has something to do with the dataset the AI has access to.” Because preprints haven’t yet undergone peer review, IEEE Access considers heavy reliance on them a problem.

In addition, although the research-integrity checking tools didn’t spot any issues with figures, Mahoney did. One figure included a red line labeled with the nonsense term “lhewl,” and an AI “brain” in another figure had some random dots in it, which ironically were a tell that it was AI generated.

Automated research systems are very much a work in progress, but they are already starting to make waves in the scientific community. For instance, an AI Scientist academic paper and papers from the Autoscience Institute were accepted through double-blind peer review in 2025 by the International Conference on Learning Representations. As these systems improve and start to produce research outputs at volume, the waves are likely to build to a tsunami that will threaten today’s scientific and publishing process.

“FARS doesn’t kill the paper, but it does challenge the paper as the unit of knowledge,” argues Su. “We believe the future looks more like a living knowledge graph—where individual, well-scoped contributions (some made by humans, some by machines) connect and build on each other dynamically.”

Benjamin Skuse's experiment raised a bigger question: What counts as legitimate scientific research in the age of AI?

In this future, humans will continue to have roles in the scientific and publication processes—just very different and limited ones. For example, instead of conducting experiments themselves, humans would sense-check and review automated output at key points. And traditional line-by-line peer-reviewing will be a thing of the past, though Su emphasizes that this change will not eliminate human judgment. “Automated systems can handle reproducibility checks, statistical validation, and novelty screening,” she says. “Humans can then focus on the harder question: Does this [research] matter?”

Though from a very different world than Su, Mahoney agrees that humans need to be freed to focus on the science, and that technology holds the key. “It’s promising to see the progress that has been made to automate some of the triage tasks, such as author checks, tortured phrases, duplicate submission, reference validity, et cetera,” she says. “During peer review, we’re also using AI semantic search tools to help editors match manuscripts to the most relevant reviewers, who are best placed to stop the slop before entering the scientific record.”

In addition, Mahoney thinks that AI cannot be banned or overly restricted, as this will stymie progress at a time when human knowledge could and should be growing at an unprecedented rate. “Researchers are increasingly using AI in their work, from literature discovery, to code generation, to data analysis, and this is not necessarily a bad thing,” she argues. But she disagrees that peer reviewers and humans more broadly will play a smaller part in scientific progress; Mahoney believes the future still requires humans at the wheel. The question is not just whether the research matters, she says. “The question should be: Can this work be trusted and reproduced?”

To this end, Longobardi argues that AI may ultimately require scientists to prove not just what they discovered but how they discovered it. One possibility, he says, is using technology to verify research at the source. “The system doesn’t really help because it’s not designed to not trust the paper,” he explains. “Maybe institutions can think about developing their own trust markers, automatically integrating the equipment researchers use with blockchain technology to say ‘Yes, this person was in the lab on this day and got this data.’”

Elements of this approach are already emerging. For instance, two departments within the Max Planck Institute of Colloids and Interfaces have implemented a sample database, assigning each and every sample created under their roofs with a unique ID and QR code. And the University of Southampton’s School of Chemistry and Chemical Engineering has rolled out an electronic lab notebook system. These innovative safeguards represent early efforts toward keeping humans front and center in scientific progress, and making the scientific process itself more transparent.

Whether this human-centric vision, Su’s AI-driven aspiration, or some other picture of the future wins out remains to be seen. The one thing my vibe-research adventure has clarified is that business-as-usual science is not an option. Scientists and publishers must adapt to a world in which it’s becoming increasingly difficult to spot the difference between real research and AI forgeries, and where deciding what counts as legitimate scientific work may become even harder than detecting outright fraud.

Benjamin Skuse created two papers for this experiment, both screened by IEEE Access with the publisher’s cooperation. Neither was accepted for publication.

Paper 1: The AI-Generated ForgeryCreated with ChatGPT and Gemini, this paper describes research that never happened.

Paper 2: The AI-Generated Research PaperCreated with Analemma’s FARS system, this paper describes computational research conducted by AI.

Neither paper was peer reviewed, and their scientific claims have not been independently validated.

Benjamin Skuse is a professional freelance writer of all things science and technology. Previously, he earned a Ph.D. in applied mathematics from the University of Edinburgh and an M.Sc. in science communication from the University of the West of England. His work has appeared in New Scientist, WIRED, Physics World, Sky & Telescope, Photonics Focus, and many more.

Summaries do go wrong, who suffers? That article describes one thread - I think the link is active for 30 days. While I think the premise of the article is valid, I have serious concerns about the use of the fake publications to test the defenses of publication process. #3277. How to Make Sure an 'Onion' Site on the Dark Web Is Legitimate

Thankfully, Tor Browser already has a cryptography-backed feature that can verify the authenticity of an onion site, by confirming whether it has end-to-end encryption and extended validation certificates. Here's how this feature works, where it falters, as well as what other red flags you should look for.

While phishing on the dark web works as it does on the clear web, scammers have a few unique advantages due to the secretive nature of the environment. Most importantly, you can’t just glance at an onion link to tell if the site is genuine. Normal website URLs tend to be short and memorable, while onion links are 56-character strings of alphanumeric text that look mostly like gibberish.

When you try to connect, Tor Browser verifies the URL against the originating website’s cryptographic key, which is how you know nobody has hijacked the address or tampered with it midway. But since this has the unwanted effect of making domains harder to recall, scammers have a much easier time generating lookalike addresses or creating website clones.

For example, many popular websites use “vanity prefixes” to make their onion addresses more easily identifiable or to add some branding appeal. That means their 56-character onion link starts with something like “facebook,” “bbcnews,” or “ciadotgov.” But scammers can use a free tool like mkp224o to generate lookalike addresses with the same vanity prefix as the legitimate website, which gives users a false sense of security.

Of course, most dark web users don’t type addresses directly into Tor Browser; they use dark web directories like the Hidden Wiki to find useful onion sites relevant to their search. Scammers will create fake search engines or link directories to point users to their fake websites, like when the Ahmia search engine discovered that a copy of its platform was directing users to 255 cloned services back in 2015.

Of course, it’s possible to orchestrate phishing attempts that don’t involve cloning sites at all. Researchers at Freie Universität Berlin describe a sophisticated technique where attackers serve the real website through their own reverse proxy, which lets them manipulate parts of the site or log your online activity without your awareness. In 2019, ESET even found a trojanized version of Tor Browser that replaced Bitcoin addresses on websites to direct payments to hackers. So both genuine websites and your browser itself are also vulnerable to manipulation if you download or access them from an unverified source.

There are a few best practices to avoid phishing attacks when using the dark web. None of them are foolproof on their own, but together, they considerably lower the risk of ending up on a fake or manipulated website.

On the desktop version of Tor Browser, you can access an onion site using a shortened version of its URL called an Onion Name. For now, this feature only works with SecureDrop, so newsrooms can establish tip lines with addresses like mysitename.securedrop.tor.onion, which would then redirect to the 56-character original onion address. This feature is in active development, so more platforms might support it in the future.

When you load up an onion site using the Tor Browser, you’ll see an onion icon on the address bar, which confirms that your connection is end-to-end encrypted. But you can also click on the onion icon to check if the site has an Extended Validation (EV) certificate, which tells you that its authenticity has been verified by a trusted certificate authority like DigiCert. While not every legitimate onion site will have an EV certificate, famous ones like Facebook tend to.

On the other hand, if you see a caution sign next to the onion icon, that means the site is using a self-signed or expired certificate that isn’t guaranteed by a trusted authority. It may also imply that the site is being served over an insecure URL. This doesn’t definitely tell you it’s a phishing site, but it’s a red flag to watch out for nevertheless.

Don’t rely on search engines, link directories, Reddit threads, or Telegram channels too heavily on the dark web. Once you’re sure you’ve found the onion address for a genuine site, bookmark it so you can access it directly the next time you want to visit.

If you realized that you’ve been the victim of a phishing attempt, the first step is to close the browser window with the fake site and access the real onion address to reset any account passwords you may have accidentally divulged.

Also, generally try to enable two-factor authentication and PGP logins on any dark web account that supports it for added security. And if you downloaded Tor Browser from anywhere other than the official Tor Project site, uninstall it now and grab a fresh copy from the official address.

#3276. If you bought an iPhone Duo, have you kept or returned it? [Poll]

When Apple announced the iPhone Duo back in September, the company called it “the most transformational change to iPhone since the original,” and there’s no doubt that it generated a huge amount of excitement.

But a new report suggests that for some buyers the novelty quickly wore off, and they ended up returning their devices. Is this just a handful of people, or is it more common … ?

It’s been a very long time since any smartphone launch has generated quite so much buzz. Apple called it a breakthrough in iPhone design.

iPhone Duo features a breakthrough foldable design that’s beautiful, versatile, and durable, opening up possibilities that feel entirely new yet remarkably familiar […]

“iPhone Duo is the most transformational change to iPhone since the original. With an entirely new design and intuitive experiences, it shows what’s possible when hardware and software are engineered together and redefines what it means to use a foldable phone,” said John Ternus.

Despite not really being the target market for the phone, I was still wowed by the launch video and remained incredibly impressed when I got some hands-on time with one.

Many couldn’t resist buying one despite the price – but The Verge notes that not everyone has ending up keeping the device. Apple allows you to return any product within 14 days for a full refund without having to give any reason. That window has come to an end for some of the first buyers and the site’s Alison Johnson spoke with some of those who’d decided to take advantage of it.

The iPhone Duo replaced both my iPhone 15 Pro Max and my iPad Mini 6. It now is my phone and iPad mini in my pocket. This is the dream phone I never knew I wanted.

And for the lack of Face ID, Touch ID works perfect with my Apple Watch. And even without wearing it, I don’t see the big deal of the ‘huge’ effort of bringing my finger to a button.

For the lacking 5x zoom that I had on my Pro Max, I haven’t had a moment yet that I wanted to use it to be honest. Those moments will definitely arise, but the lack of that camera cannot go up against the amazing overall experience of the iPhone Duo.

But the more fundamental reason for some is that it hasn’t really lived up to their hopes for a multifunctional device.

“If I can have an iPad in my pocket, that would be great.” So thought Ben Seligson, a content creator, photographer, and now former iPhone Duo owner […] “Usually I’d throw a YouTube video on the iPad or throw a podcast up. And then I start cooking dinner and leave my iPad in one spot, but I’d have my phone in my pocket if I got a text, or I needed to set a timer or something like that.” With the Duo, the phone was also the iPad on the counter, so a quick reply became much more of an interruption.

I’m curious as to whether this is just a small minority of buyers or a more common phenomenon. If you bought a Duo early enough to have hit the end of the return window, please take our poll to let us know whether you decided to keep it or return it – and do share your reasons in the comments (which are now back).

Oh, and the good news for anyone buying one now is that you’ll have a lot longer to make up your mind, with the extended return window for the holidays in place. You can now return anything bought today through January 8.
